title: The Hidden Cost of Cancelling NEET-UG 2026

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Cancelling NEET-UG 2026
detail.abstract: The National Testing Agency cancelled the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test, Undergraduate (NEET-UG) examination of 3 May 2026 after evidence of a paper leak, and held a fresh examination on 21 June. Registration data carried forward unchanged, so agency records show how many registered candidates chose not to sit the second examination. About 12% stayed away, roughly four times the rate of the three preceding years. Around 2.17 lakh more candidates were absent than recent experience predicts, and the shortfall was uneven. Kerala and Tamil Nadu recorded rates near 25%, while Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan stayed below 8%. Women stayed away at a higher rate than men, reversing the earlier pattern. The Joint Entrance Examination, Main (JEE-Main), conducted by the same agency in the same year, shows no comparable break from its own trend. The evidence is descriptive and identifies no mechanism, but it does establish that re-conducting the examination carried a substantial cost of lost participation.

title: Evaluation of Policy-Relevant Forecasting Advantage of Machine and Deep Learning Models over Classical Econometrics: Evidence from Ghanaian Headline Inflation
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development. Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training den Entrepreneurial Development,, University of Bradford and Transilvania University of Brasov

detail.title: Evaluation of Policy-Relevant Forecasting Advantage of Machine and Deep Learning Models over Classical Econometrics: Evidence from Ghanaian Headline Inflation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates whether machine learning and deep learning models offer a genuine forecasting advantage over classical econometric benchmarks for Ghana's headline (year-on-year) inflation, a question of direct relevance to a central bank operating an inflation-targeting regime in a small, commodity-exposed, currency-volatile economy. Using 280 months (January 2000-April 2023) of Bank of Ghana monetary and macro-financial data, we construct a strictly one-step-ahead forecasting matrix in which every predictor reflects information available one month before the forecast target, and compare nine models (a random walk and seasonal naive baseline, an AIC-selected ARIMA benchmark, two regularized linear models [Ridge, Lasso], two tree ensembles [Random Forest, XGBoost], a kernel method [Support Vector Regression], and a shallow feed-forward neural network) on a chronological train/validation/test split whose 42-month test window (October 2019-April 2023) deliberately spans Ghana's 2022-23 inflation surge. Contrary to the presumption that more flexible models dominate, the ARIMA(3,1,0) benchmark achieved the lowest test-set RMSE (2.41 percentage points), narrowly ahead of the random walk (2.65) and Lasso (3.41). However, Diebold-Mariano tests show that ARIMA is not statistically distinguishable from either of these two closest competitors, while its advantage over every other model is statistically significant. Every nonlinear machine learning model underperformed both simple baselines out of sample, with several models (notably XGBoost and the neural network) showing a large gap between near-perfect training fit and poor test performance: a textbook overfitting signature accentuated by the regime shift embedded in the test period. We argue this is a genuine and policy-relevant finding rather than a failure of specification: headline inflation is highly persistent, and models that best exploit that persistence, rather than those with the greatest functional flexibility, forecast best through a structural break. The study details a leakage-free feature-engineering protocol, reports full hyperparameter-tuning and diagnostic results, and discusses the conditions, such as larger samples, richer nonlinear feature sets, or regime-aware architectures, under which machine learning might be expected to add value for inflation forecasting in a market such as Ghana's.

title: Acting to Believe
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Acting to Believe
detail.abstract: Can people build confidence simply by misremembering the past, or must they act to earn it? We examine these two routes in a field experiment with university students completing two rounds of self-control tasks. Before the second round, students were randomly assigned to receive no reminder, an expected reminder, or an unexpected reminder of first-round performance. Reminders correct potential memory bias and separate confidence generated by biased recall from confidence generated by effort. Students without reminders formed a positive memory bias, recalling first-round performance as better than it was, but this bias did not robustly increase confidence or second-task participation relative to the unexpected-reminder group. In contrast, students expecting a reminder exerted significantly more first-round effort, then reported higher confidence in self-control and participated more in the second task. We develop an intrapersonal self-signaling model driven by either a self-regulation or a self-image motive. Our findings support the self-regulation motive.

title:
FROM MASSERA TO INFANTINO
Were World Cups Fixed in Argentina's Favor?

detail.title:
FROM MASSERA TO INFANTINO
Were World Cups Fixed in Argentina's Favor?
detail.abstract:
The relationship between Argentina and the World Cup contains two historical moments in which sporting success was surrounded by an extraordinarily problematic institutional structure. In 1978, the tournament was organized by a dictatorship that used the championship as an instrument of internal legitimation and international propaganda. The 6–0 victory over Peru remains the object of suspicion, testimony, and hypotheses of political intervention, although the available public record lacks the documentation needed to establish a fixed match conclusively. Between the two poles, the presidency of Joseph Blatter (1998–2015) left the systemic corruption of the FIFA apparatus proven, with individual responsibilities fragmented between internal ethics sanctions and criminal acquittals. Between 2022 and 2026 a different configuration appears: a statistically extraordinary concentration of penalties and favorable decisions, combined with an opaque international organization, commercially dependent on Lionel Messi and capable of relaxing disciplinary procedures under political pressure.
Argentina was awarded eight penalties in twelve World Cup matches between Qatar 2022 and the 2026 round of 16, a figure that became eight in thirteen after the quarterfinal against Switzerland. That match added no penalties, but it did add another favorable decision of maximum impact: the second yellow card and sending-off of Breel Embolo following a VAR intervention, with the match level and Switzerland in its best stretch. In Qatar, Argentina received five penalties, a record for a single team in one edition. In 2026 a second series accumulated: three penalties in the first five matches, one booking per 19.7 fouls through the round of 16, the absence of any relevant sanction against Messi for a challenge comparable to others punished with a sending-off, and several borderline decisions of high impact against Egypt and Switzerland.
This paper separates three planes that public discussion tends to blur: statistical anomaly,institutional favoritism, and deliberate coordination. Thefirstis real and measurable. The second is documented off the pitch through the inclusion of Inter Miami in the Club World Cup, the disciplinary elasticity applied to commercially valuable figures, and the political intervention surrounding Folarin Balogun’s sanction. The public celebration of Infantino alongside Claudio Tapia and Alejandro Domínguez after the win over Cape Verde further degraded the appearance of neutrality. Deliberate coordination of refereeing decisions, by contrast, remains undemonstrated: communications, payments, instructions, trace ability of appointments, and internal testimony are all missing.

title: Do climate policy uncertainty and artificial intelligence matter in energy markets? A quantile-frequency connectedness analysis for China and the U.S
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Business School, Shandong University, Shandong University at Weihai and University of Wollongong

detail.title: Do climate policy uncertainty and artificial intelligence matter in energy markets? A quantile-frequency connectedness analysis for China and the U.S
detail.abstract: This study  proposes  a quantile and frequency connectedness network based on GARCH-MIDAS decomposition to investigate the state-dependent and horizon-specific spillover dynamics among climate policy uncertainty (CPU), artificial intelligence (AI), and energy markets in China and the United States. The results reveal strong state dependence within the CPU-AI-Energy system, with total connectedness rising significantly under both lower- and upper-tail market conditions, indicating stronger systemic synchronization during extreme periods. Frequency decomposition further shows that long-run spillovers dominate persistent systemic dependence, while short-run transmission mainly reflects temporary market adjustment. The analysis further reveals substantial cross-country heterogeneity. China’s climate policy uncertainty primarily contributes through persistent transmission, whereas U.S. climate policy uncertainty becomes more influential under stressed market conditions. AI displays heterogeneous transmission patterns across countries and horizons, with more active transmission under favorable market conditions. Energy markets predominantly function as shock absorbers, although responses vary across assets and frequencies. Cross-country interactions intensify under extreme conditions, highlighting the growing importance of international transmission and structural adjustment processes. Through a comparison between the U.S. and China, this study provides context-specific insights for systemic risk assessment and cross-market shock diagnostics in an increasingly AI-influenced global energy landscape.

title: Natural Disasters, Health and Recovery around the World
affiliations: International Institute of Social Studies of Erasmus University and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Institute of Social Studies (ISS)

detail.title: Natural Disasters, Health and Recovery around the World
detail.abstract: A substantial share of the world’s children resides in disaster-prone areas and suffers from stunted growth. Child growth in the first 1000 days of life can falter depending on health endowments, shocks and investments. We investigate growth faltering and catch-up in children exposed to comparable earthquakes in utero. Our analysis leverages georeferenced health and earthquake data from almost a million children under the age of five across 55 countries. Our preferred models exploit within cluster or mother variation and control for temporal trends. On average, we document adverse effects on children's height that are more pronounced when earthquakes are more unexpected and higher in magnitude. These average effects, however, conceal negative short-term effects and recovery mechanisms via parental health investments and economic recouping, alongside correlational evidence on development assistance, which coincide with subsequent catch-up growth. We discuss our findings and contributions within the literature on child health and disasters, which is relatively sparse on the analysis of post-disaster recovery mechanisms and has largely been confined to single-country studies.

title: The Recipient on Both Sides: Section 504 and the Two Harms Only a University Can Produce with a License Plate Camera

detail.title: The Recipient on Both Sides: Section 504 and the Two Harms Only a University Can Produce with a License Plate Camera
detail.abstract: At least one hundred fifty American colleges and universities have connected their campuses to a private, nationwide automated license plate recognition network. The civil liberties literature treats this as a privacy, immigration, and First Amendment problem. It is also a disability discrimination problem, and no institution has been asked to answer for it. This Article argues that campus deployment violates Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act through two mechanisms that exist only in higher education. The first is documentary. The federal uniform system for disability parking puts the International Symbol of Access on the face of a special license plate, sized like the plate's own characters and physician-certified, which places a disability marker in the exact field the reader is built to capture. A municipality that photographs that field holds a photograph. A university holds the parking permit registry that maps every plate on its grounds to a name and an address, so the same photograph resolves to a person. The register is not built by decision. It is what one covered entity can assemble from components it already holds, and only a university holds all of them. The second is therapeutic, and it must be stated in the terms the clinical literature uses. Contemporary treatment for persecutory delusions does not proceed by presenting counterevidence, an approach that literature has long regarded as unproductive. It proceeds by helping the person learn, through direct experience, that a feared threat is not present. For persecutory belief that takes the common form of a conviction that one is being watched or followed, the learning target is a proposition about the environment, and on a networked campus that proposition is not available to be learned because it is false in the one respect the treatment must address. The university that operates the counseling center delivering that intervention is the same entity that operates the camera network, inside a single program or activity, because Section 504 defines that term to reach all of the operations of a postsecondary institution. In the municipal fact pattern the camera operator and the clinician are different entities. On a campus they are the same defendant, and the population is concentrated at the age of peak incidence. Section 504 is the correct instrument rather than Title II because a substantial share of the deploying institutions are private and outside Title II altogether. The Article maps the claim onto the discriminatory methods of administration and facility siting provisions, notes that the definition of facility expressly includes equipment and parking lots, addresses the vendor as a contractual arrangement rather than a shield, adds a failure-to-accommodate theory that does not depend on the contested availability of disparate impact, identifies a modification the vendor has already stated it is implementing under state law, and locates the surviving damages theory after recent limits on compensatory relief.

title: Delisting Finance and Servicing
affiliations: Democritus University of Thrace, Law School

detail.title: Delisting Finance and Servicing
detail.abstract: The article provides a legal assessment of the pivotal and often instigatory role of credit institutions in the growing voluntary delistings from European regulated markets. This phenomenon signals a reversal of the traditional shift from bank-based to capital market-based financing, positioning banks not merely as financiers, but as architects and sponsors of these complex corporate transactions. The analysis dissects the multifarious engagement of banks, commencing with the provision of structured acquisition finance (typically to dominant shareholders or special purpose vehicles-SPVs) designed to fund the buyout of minority shareholdings. It examines the intricate contractual frameworks of such credit facilities, which are engineered to mitigate credit risk through mechanisms including the "push-down" of acquisition debt onto the target entity (postdelisting), or, alternatively, through stringent covenants compelling expeditious repayment from the target's operational cash flows (if delisting proves unsuccessful). This analysis is contextualized within the architecture of EU company and capital markets law, particularly the prohibitions and rules on financial assistance, takeover bids and squeeze-out regimes. Beyond debt provision, the article elucidates the ancillary advisory and transactional services rendered by banks-including the issuance of fairness opinions and the certification of a bidder's financial capacity-which are indispensable to the execution of such operations. A significant portion of the discourse is dedicated to the attendant legal complexities and risks inherent in those bank activities. Two principal areas of concern are identified: first, the potential conflicts of interest emanating from the banks' diverse and sometimes antagonistic mandates as lenders, advisors, underwriters, asset managers, and proprietary traders; and second, the potential for contravention of the EU market abuse regime, given that the delisting strategy and its associated financing invariably constitute pricesensitive inside information. The article posits that while this deep involvement in delisting projects signifies a strategic resurgence for the banking sector, its future prospects are to be influenced significantly by the macroeconomic environment (interest rates) and market evolutions. Simultaneously, it proposes the implementation of robust internal governance and compliance mechanisms by the engaged banks and financial institutions, so that they mitigate all involved regulatory, litigation and reputational risks, effectively.

title: The Constitutional Architecture of Catastrophe: How Sudan's 2019 Charter Enabled the RSF's Rise and the 2023 Civil War
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Constitutional Architecture of Catastrophe: How Sudan's 2019 Charter Enabled the RSF's Rise and the 2023 Civil War

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The subject is an important part of my research
declarations.ethicsApproval: I am the author of the paper
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

keywords: Parallel Army / Dual-Army Structure. Weak Accountability Mechanisms

detail.abstract: The paper offers a comprehensive critical analysis of Sudan's 2019 Constitutional Document, arguing that its foundational compromises-far from being a neutral framework for democratic transition-contained structural flaws that directly enabled the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to accumulate power and ultimately launch the civil war of 2023. Drawing on constitutional theory, conflict studies, and empirical evidence from the transition period, the paper demonstrates that the Charter's legitimization of a parallel military structure, its weak provisions for security sector integration, its power-sharing formula that institutionalized military veto authority, and its failure to establish credible accountability mechanisms created what scholars term "nominal constitutionalism"-a formal text that served as a hollow veneer for the unfettered exercise of military power (Saeed, 2026). By examining the Charter's constitutional architecture, this paper demonstrates that the Sudanese war is not merely a failure of implementation but a direct consequence of the constitutional choices made in 2019. These choices reflected a fundamental misunderstanding of the dynamics of military power in post-authoritarian transitions (Tran, 2023). The analysis incorporates comparative constitutional perspectives from post-Arab Spring transitions and examines the role of donor conditionality in shaping the Charter's flawed economic and governance provisions (Ali, Alneel, & Hassanain, 2025).

title: Is Data Privacy a Losing Game? Evidence from Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) Policy
affiliations: Joint Research Centre - European Commission, University of Cambridge, Cambridge Judge Business School and

detail.title: Is Data Privacy a Losing Game? Evidence from Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) Policy
detail.abstract: We study the impact of Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) policy, which requires apps to obtain explicit user permission before cross-app tracking, on the mobile gaming industry. Using SensorTower US data on the top 5,000 games on iOS and Android (2020-2023) and a difference-indifferences design, we show that ATT increases iOS games' revenue and revenue per user, with little impact on user numbers. Gains arise from re-optimised in-app purchase menus and more major updates, not higher prices or paywalls. ATT raises concentration and reduces entry, benefiting Apple and incumbents while raising barriers to entry for new competitors.

title: Analysis of the Efficiency of using QRIS in the Management of MSMEs
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: Analysis of the Efficiency of using QRIS in the Management of MSMEs
detail.abstract:
Although they are essential to the country's economy, small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) frequently struggle with operational financial management. A key tool in advancing the digitalization of this industry is the Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard (QRIS), a cashless payment standard based on QR codes. The purpose of this article is to examine the effectiveness of employing QRIS in SME management, with a particular emphasis on transaction time efficiency, financial record-keeping accuracy, and operational cost reduction.

A survey of the literature and a contextual analysis of several digital payment methods and SME operational management practices are used in the analysis. In comparison to traditional cash payment methods, the study focuses on assessing the effects of incorporating QRIS-based digital payment systems.

According to the analysis, QRIS installation greatly improves the operational efficiency of SMEs. It has been demonstrated that using QRIS speeds up transaction procedures, reduces the hazards associated with handling cash (such fake money or improper change), and makes it easier to compile financial reports automatically and in real time. However, issues including low digital literacy among business owners, network infrastructure constraints, and settlement delays continue to hinder its efficiency. All things considered, the implementation of QRIS is a successful strategic step toward modernizing SME management and promoting a more diverse digital financial ecosystem.

title: "Defying Volatility: An Analysis of Large-scale Firm Stability in Pakistan's Emerging Market"
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: "Defying Volatility: An Analysis of Large-scale Firm Stability in Pakistan's Emerging Market"
detail.abstract: This research examines how large-scale enterprises (LSEs) in Pakistan sustain industrial stability and profitability despite a volatile macroeconomic environment characterized by persistent inflation and political instability. The study seeks to identify the specific internal organizational drivers and management maneuvers that allow these firms to defy conventional predictions of firm-level instability during economic downturns. Through the utilization of a qualitative multi-sectoral research design, the study employed semi-structured interviews with "positional elites", CEOs and senior executives, across six diverse industrial sectors, including manufacturing, textiles, and food services. The findings reveal that stability is maintained through the process of "proactive decoupling," where instead of moving alongside a country's external environment, a firm makes measures to separate their internal performance. Decoupling breaks the dependency between the firm's success and economic health. This is possible through technology hedging, including labor automation and renewable energy transformation, coupled with market economies of scale. Stability, as such, has become increasingly more institutionalized as the adaptation of technology and internal standards act as defence from economic fluctuations. The study presents Pillars of Stability that can be referred to in order to study how mass stabilization of business operating in an emerging market can be achieved. With an ultimate call for a paradigm shift from reactive expense reduction to more proactive decision making.

title: Towards Autonomous Sustainability in Electronics Supply Chains: A Systematic Review and Agentic AI-driven Conceptual Framework for Green Supply Chain Resilience

detail.title: Towards Autonomous Sustainability in Electronics Supply Chains: A Systematic Review and Agentic AI-driven Conceptual Framework for Green Supply Chain Resilience
detail.abstract: This study examines the role of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) in transforming green supply chain resilience in the dynamic electronics and semiconductor industry. Predictive AI is widely adopted in supply chain management; however, the critical challenge of bridging data-driven decisions and independent actions remains. To resolve this challenge, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) adopting the PRISMA 2020 protocol was applied, analyzing 170 peer-reviewed articles published between 2020 and 2026. The SLR reveals accelerating research into autonomous systems for sustainable supply chain management, yet this body of work remains largely generic and industry-agnostic. Sector-specific deployment that balances efficiency and sustainability remains under-researched. Thus, the study proposes an ASR Framework based on dynamic capabilities and resource management theory. It consists of three layers: autonomous sensing, goal-oriented orchestration, and decentralized execution. This framework emphasizes the role of agentic systems in improving environmental and operational performance. Finally, the study presents research hypotheses and a strategic plan to realize human-centered, Industry 5.0-oriented supply chain systems in the electronics and semiconductor sector.

title: Two Estimands, One Identity: Equilibrium-Implied Electricity Demand from Bitcoin Mining at Coin Prices of $1-$10 Million
affiliations: University of Exeter

detail.title: Two Estimands, One Identity: Equilibrium-Implied Electricity Demand from Bitcoin Mining at Coin Prices of $1-$10 Million
detail.abstract: Estimates of Bitcoin mining's electricity use disagree by an order of magnitude, and are usually read as uncertainty about one quantity. They are not. The engineering literature estimates electricity from observed hashpower and an assumed fleet-efficiency distribution; the expenditure literature computes the electricity revenue implies, given a tariff and cost decomposition. We show the two coincide if and only if revenue equals total economic cost, and away from that locus stand in the exact ratio E R /E H = R/C. In one miner's filings the same electricity expenditure reproduces under all five disclosed cost denominators while R/C ranges from 0.61 to 1.72, so the reported spread is a range of cost concepts not of electricity. Chain data cannot close the gap: observed hashpower and revenue place one restriction on three unknowns, and the deficiency does not fall with length. Replacing the assumed coordinates with disclosed ones, we assemble tariffs and cost shares from filings, screen them against the hardware record, and evaluate the schedule at coin prices of one to ten million dollars. The surface is exactly linear in price; under the constant-share baseline it steps down on each halving. At one million dollars a coin the implied electricity in 2027 is 2,247 TWh, about 6.6 per cent of projected world generation; the requirement, not a forecast, is the informative object. The single most valuable disclosure would be the effective economic life of a mining fleet, which no filing reports and would narrow the capital-cost uncertainty.

title: Strategic Public Debt Management and Fiscal Sustainability in Developing Economies A Markov Decision Process and Dynamic Panel Analysis for African and Latin American Economies, 1995-2025
affiliations: University of Ain Temouchent, University of Ain Temouchent and

detail.title: Strategic Public Debt Management and Fiscal Sustainability in Developing Economies A Markov Decision Process and Dynamic Panel Analysis for African and Latin American Economies, 1995-2025
detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic dimensions of public debt management in developing economies by integrating Markov Decision Processes (MDP) with dynamic panel econometrics. Applying this unified framework to an unbalanced panel of 45 African and Latin American economies over the period 1995–2025, we characterise optimal debt policy as a sequential decision problem in which governments choose among borrowing strategies, fiscal consolida tion, and debt restructuring signals in response to evolving fiscal regime states. Estimation of a three-state Markov transition matrix reveals substantial hysteresis in fiscal regimes: the probability of remaining in the high-debt state exceeds 0.67, underscoring the self-reinforcing nature of debt distress in the sample. System-GMM estimates confirm that primary balance improvements exert a large and statistically robust negative effect on debt accumulation (coeffi cient −0.486, p < 0.01), while fiscal rules and institutional quality function as complementary mechanisms that reduce both the level and volatility of sovereign spreads. The MDP value function demonstrates that the payoff to proactive debt management is substantially higher under low and medium fiscal risk states, implying a significant option value of early action. Robustness checks across sub-samples, alternative estimators, and time windows confirm the stability of the core findings. The framework extends and refines existing MDP applications in sovereign debt (Cuadra et al., 2010; Arellano, 2008) by explicitly accounting for debt composi tion heterogeneity—distinguishing domestic from external and concessional from commercial debt—and by embedding fiscal rules as endogenous state-contingent constraints. Policy impli cations emphasise the importance of debt composition management, fiscal rule adoption, and institutional strengthening as complements rather than substitutes in the pursuit of long-run fiscal sustainability.

title: The Slow Erosion: Measuring Sovereignty Creep in Hong Kong under One Country, Two Systems, 1997-2024

detail.title: The Slow Erosion: Measuring Sovereignty Creep in Hong Kong under One Country, Two Systems, 1997-2024
detail.abstract: Between 1997 and 2024, Hong Kong formally retained One Country, Two Systems autonomy under the Basic Law, yet indicators of effective sovereignty declined sharply. This paper examines that decline as sovereignty creep: the legally mediated expansion of Beijing's effective competence into domains formally reserved for the HKSAR without amending the Basic Law. Applying the Burke Sovereignty Index (BSI) with open data and structured expert elicitation, it scores Hong Kong across seven observation years tied to NPCSC interpretations, the 2020 National Security Law, curriculum reform, and the 2024 Article 23 Ordinance. Political erosion begins after 1999 and 2004 interpretations; informational collapse follows the NSL; cultural decline is lagged; cognitive change is most inertial. The NSL marks a phase transition in the BSI composite score, not merely accelerated continuity. By 2022, Hong Kong's political and informational BSI scores converge toward mainland China's profile, quantifying the erosion of the two systems arrangement.

title: A Realist-Informed Causal Machine Learning Approach for Exploring and Explaining Treatment Effect Heterogeneity

detail.title: A Realist-Informed Causal Machine Learning Approach for Exploring and Explaining Treatment Effect Heterogeneity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received in relation to this research.

detail.abstract: Causal machine learning methods that can flexibly explore treatment effect heterogeneity are growing in adoption. However, despite their technical sophistication, users still struggle to draw out useful findings using these tools. They can show who benefits more or less, but not why this is. This paper argues that causal machine learning methods would benefit from the adoption of a methodology that can flexibly explain effects, not just test pre-specified hypotheses. It proposes a realist-informed approach that recasts estimates of heterogeneous treatment effects as a source of demi-regularities that point to underlying mechanisms that generate this variation. These demi-regularities are not the end product of research, but inform a process of retroductive inquiry-investigation of the underlying mechanisms generating these differences in efficacy. This means causal machine learning is used to map out how treatment effects vary, and retroduction is used to explain why this is the case. The approach is demonstrated with the stylised, fictional example of an educational reform that puts in place a problem-based numeracy curriculum in Australian schools.

title: Constraint Geometry of Institutional Synchronization

detail.title: Constraint Geometry of Institutional Synchronization
detail.abstract: Market synchronization can emerge independent of contemporaneous information arrival, driven instead by the common component of institutional optimization under shared constraints. This paper develops the constraint geometry of that mechanism, introducing three theoretical objects. First, the ISTadmissible constraint class-institutional constraint functions that admit a Common-Idiosyncratic Decomposition, delineating the scope of Institutional Synchronization Theory (IST) as a definitional rather than assumptional restriction. Second, Synchronization Pressure-a vector-valued theoretical primitive derived from constraint shadow prices and common gradients, invariant to how the econometrician projects returns. Third, the Synchronization Law-a monotonic relationship between the equilibrium pressure-aligned covariance shift and the capacity-adjusted Synchronization Pressure normalized by market capacity, derived from a minimal Kyle-style linear price-impact assumption. A single Dominance Principle unifies the four established transmission channels of institutional finance-benchmarktracking, VaR, ETF creation/redemption, and short-sale constraints-as regime-specific corollaries. The Law's linearization recovers the empirical Scaling Law documented in Yang (2026b), building on the theoretical framework of Yang (2026a); preliminary cross-market calibration is consistent with universality.

title: Why Similar Cost Pressures Result in Different Levels of Cost Misperformance in Infrastructure Projects: Protective and Passive Hand Response Logics
affiliations: Curtin University - School of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

detail.title: Why Similar Cost Pressures Result in Different Levels of Cost Misperformance in Infrastructure Projects: Protective and Passive Hand Response Logics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Infrastructure projects facing similar cost pressures often show varying degrees of cost misperformance. The dominant explanation attributes cost misperformance to the Planning Fallacy, which holds that unrealistic budgets stem primarily from optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation during an infrastructure project's planning and development. Although this perspective explains why projects start with unrealistic budgets, it offers limited insight into why projects under comparable conditions subsequently experience different levels of cost misperformance. The Fifth Hand is a burgeoning behavioral-institutional theory that explains how patterns of project behavior influence project performance through four response logics: Malevolent, Benevolent, Protective, and Passive Hands. While the Malevolent and Benevolent Hands have attracted growing scholarly attention, the Protective and Passive Hands have not been examined empirically. We address this gap through a comparative qualitative case study of four large-scale Australian infrastructure projects. Our study advances the Fifth Hand by providing the first empirical examination of the Protective and Passive Hands, developing two theoretically derived propositions that explain the institutional arrangements associated with these logics, and offering practical guidance for infrastructure governance.

title: The Corrective Disclosure in Securities Litigation
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW) - UNSW Law & Justice

detail.title: The Corrective Disclosure in Securities Litigation
detail.abstract:
The Corrective Disclosure in Securities Litigation

In order to plead and ultimately prove loss causation, a fraud-on-the-market plaintiff must identify a corrective disclosure that reveals the fraud to the market, followed by a decline in the price of the security. This Article aims to resolve a question that has divided the circuit courts: what qualifies an event to be a corrective disclosure for purposes of pleading and proving loss causation? An analysis based on first principles of tort law concludes that an event is corrective if it is systematically related to the defendant’s fraud and a factual cause of the stock price decline on which the plaintiff’s loss causation theory is predicated. An event that is a factual cause of the price decline, but not systematically related to the fraud, is an independent intervening event. It breaks the causal chain and supersedes the defendant’s fraud as the proximate cause of the plaintiff’s loss. The tort approach has a valid legal basis. The U.S. Supreme Court in Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo counseled lower courts to interpret loss causation in accordance with common law tort principles. However, lower courts have not followed the Supreme Court’s counsel. Instead, courts have interpreted Dura as requiring the plaintiff to identify a corrective disclosure that reveals the “relevant truth” and resets the artificially inflated stock price. The equivocal concept of “relevant truth” has divided the lower courts on what makes an event corrective. The division is so stark that a particular fact pattern may result in complete summary judgment for the defendant in one circuit, while the same pattern would result in denial of summary judgment, and potentially a lengthy and expensive trial, in another circuit. The approach presented in this Article reduces the equivocality by abstracting away from a focus on case-specific particulars that have divided the courts. There is greater unity among the circuits on the principles of tort than on the meaning of “relevant truth.”

title: The Challenges Confronting Aceh Government in Optimizing Its Soft Power for Aceh’s Development
affiliations: , Universiti Malaysia Terengganu (UMT) and Universiti Malaysia Terengganu (UMT)

detail.title: The Challenges Confronting Aceh Government in Optimizing Its Soft Power for Aceh’s Development
detail.abstract: This study examines the challenges faced by the Government of Aceh in optimizing soft power through paradiplomacy to support regional development. Using a qualitative phenomenological approach, data were collected through in-depth interviews with government officials, institutional actors, and stakeholders involved in international cooperation. The findings show that Aceh possesses strong soft power resources, including Islamic cultural heritage, post-conflict peace values, natural resources, and strategic geographic positioning. However, their use remains limited by conflict legacies, security concerns, weak central government trust, inadequate infrastructure, limited human resources, low technological capacity, poor digital diplomacy, bureaucratic barriers, and constitutional restrictions. The study also finds that Aceh's paradiplomacy focuses on development, cultural diplomacy, and international cooperation rather than separatist ambitions. Strengthening institutional capacity, infrastructure, digital communication, and central-regional trust is therefore essential. This study contributes to research on soft power and subnational diplomacy by showing how post-conflict regions can use paradiplomacy to promote peacebuilding and sustainable development.

title: Allocating Property Rights: Extraction without Development in Cambodia
affiliations: , Duke University, China Foreign Affairs University and

detail.title: Allocating Property Rights: Extraction without Development in Cambodia
detail.abstract: How do states allocate natural resources, and why do some allocations generate extraction rather than development? We study Cambodia's economic land concessions (ELCs), which transformed state-controlled land into privately enforceable commercial rights. Combining spatial and cohort-based difference-indifferences designs with international rubber-price shocks interacted with predetermined suitability, we examine how resource rents are converted into property-right allocation and local outcomes. We find that ELCs increased forest loss both within concession boundaries and across receiving districts, while generating no comparable local development dividend: nighttime activity did not increase at project sites and even declined in pre-existing settlements. International rent exposure increased new concession grants after an administrative delay, and the same exposure produced greater extraction and weaker local development. Historical legacies conditioned where extraction intensified. The findings show that property-right formalization can facilitate resource extraction without broad-based development when states allocate enforceable rights to actors with limited local economic linkages.

title: Carbon Pricing and Corporate Biodiversity Footprints: Environmental Co-Benefits and Resource Use Trade-Offs
affiliations: University of St Andrews - School of Management, Khatam University and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: Carbon Pricing and Corporate Biodiversity Footprints: Environmental Co-Benefits and Resource Use Trade-Offs
detail.abstract: This paper examines how carbon pricing affects corporate biodiversity footprints using firm-level panel data from 2018-2024. Because such policies target greenhouse gas emissions, their broader biodiversity effects are theoretically ambiguous: cleaner production may reduce pollution and land use pressures, while the lowcarbon transition may intensify resource extraction. Exploiting Washington State's Cap-and-Invest Program as a quasi-experimental shock, we estimate difference-indifferences effects across biodiversity-pressure categories. We find that carbon pricing reduces firms' overall biodiversity footprints by about 16.5%, driven by reductions in pressures associated with greenhouse gas emissions, land use, air pollution, and water pollution. In contrast, resource-related pressures increase, consistent with greater material demand during the transition. These reductions in biodiversity pressures are stronger among firms with higher pre-treatment emissions intensity, but weaker among rapidly growing firms. Overall, carbon pricing generates broad environmental co-benefits but also creates resource use trade-offs.

keywords: Out-Of-Pocket Healthcare Expenditure Health Financing Catastrophic Health Expenditure Asia-Pacific Universal Health Coverage GDP Per Capita Health Policy

detail.abstract:
This paper is based on a study which investigates the determinants of out-of-pocket health expenditures across 30 nations of the Asia Pacific. I have employed an OLS regression model to examine how different macroeconomic variables affect the OOP-expenditure. The model includes variables like government health expenditure, physician density, NCD burden, out of which GDP per capita is the statistically significant predictor of financial burden of healthcare on households.
The model’s outlier analysis reveals that income is also an incomplete metric for the expenditure measurement. Thailand and Japan outperform what was expected by them as per model predictions, reducing their OOP expenditure by 31 and 15 percentage points respectively. Whereas countries like Bangladesh and Turkmenistan underperform the economic predictions as their OOP expenditure costs go over 33 percentage points than what was expected. India surprisingly sits right on the predicted score.
This analysis concludes that while economic growth is a crucial factor in minimizing the OOP expenditures, it would perform weakly if not complemented by good policy interventions. If a country wants to provide financial healthcare protection to the citizens, it must design policies which build a financial safety net for the expenditure shocks to the citizens. Economic development and growth are important tools to ensure the comfort of the citizens, but better financial systems will determine if the citizens are protected from catastrophic expenditure or not.

title: The Selection Criterion: Attenuated Design, Sequence Evidence, and What Deregulation Cannot Explain About Federal Several Rights Policy

detail.title: The Selection Criterion: Attenuated Design, Sequence Evidence, and What Deregulation Cannot Explain About Federal Several Rights Policy
detail.abstract: Between December 2025 and July 2026 the federal government took four discrete actions narrowing civil rights enforcement, each accompanied by a neutral administrative justification. This article argues those justifications are insufficient on their own terms, and that the insufficiency is demonstrable without proving animus toward any protected class. A deregulatory rationale predicts contraction distributed across an agency's functions. What the record shows is something narrower and harder to answer. The Department deregulated across its portfolio in this period, but it ran a public negotiated rulemaking committee on accreditation and notice and comment rulemaking on student loans, while the four civil rights actions took no public process at all and two of them were effective on publication. The contraction was not confined to civil rights; the absence of procedure was. That occurred alongside the first nationwide federal program subsidizing private elementary and secondary schooling, an expansion that as a matter of Free Exercise doctrine reaches religious schools. Selective contraction paired with a single expansion is reallocation, and reallocation rests on a criterion the stated rationales do not supply. The article develops the federal tax credit scholarship program as the analytically decisive instrument on three grounds. First, its architecture reproduces what political scientists have documented as attenuated design: the deliberate routing of public money through private intermediaries and the tax system, a technique whose recorded origin is the effort by southern legislatures to insulate segregation tuition grants from judicial challenge. Second, private schools receiving such funds may lawfully discriminate on disability, so the instrument removes children from the statutory regime built for them. Third, the tax credit structure is plausibly designed to keep receiving schools outside the federal financial assistance trigger on which Title VI, Section 504, and Title IX all depend. The article engages the substantial scholarly dispute over how far the segregationist origins of vouchers extend, and shows that the argument advanced here survives the strongest revisionist account. The claim developed is an arbitrary and capricious claim under the Administrative Procedure Act rather than an equal protection claim, a placement that lets pretext evidence assembled under Village of Arlington Heights operate on the administrative record without requiring a court to assign a tier of scrutiny to any class.

title: Pricing Options on Illiquid Assets Using Liquid Market Benchmarks: An Application to Energy Markets
affiliations: , University of Rome II, University of Rome Tor Vergata - Department of Economics and Finance and

detail.title: Pricing Options on Illiquid Assets Using Liquid Market Benchmarks: An Application to Energy Markets

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Gasoil options market is illiquid, making it difficult to construct its implied volatility surface directly. However, it is closely linked to the highly liquid Brent options market. In this paper, we jointly model Brent and Gasoil futures prices through a correlated Bachelier local volatility model: the Brent factor is described by a normal mixture diffusion model, while the Gasoil-Brent spot volatility spread is estimated using a data-driven procedure that identifies clusters of historical crack-spread levels and Gasoil-Brent volatility spreads. The resulting bivariate model allows us to compute an implied volatility correction that maps Brent implied volatilities to Gasoil implied volatilities without using illiquid Gasoil option prices as inputs. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the resulting implied volatilities closely match observed Gasoil implied volatilities when benchmarked against more direct approaches. These results suggest that the proposed framework is well suited for modeling refined products and pricing the corresponding financial derivatives.

title: The Hidden Clocks of Leadership: Subordinates' Horizon and Corporate Financial Distress Risk
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and School of Accounting, Xijing University

detail.title: The Hidden Clocks of Leadership: Subordinates' Horizon and Corporate Financial Distress Risk
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether key subordinate executives' horizon affects corporate financial distress risk. Using a unique sample of 18,174 US firm-year observations from 1998 to 2022, we document that an increase in subordinate executives' horizon is associated with higher financial distress risk, measured using distance to default. These findings hold across alternative measures of subordinate executives' horizon and financial distress risk, alternative econometric specifications, and subsample analyses. The results are also robust to several identification strategies. Channel analysis indicates that financial constraints, CEO power, and corporate governance strength moderate this relationship. These findings contribute to the literature on top management teams and firm risk. They show that subordinate executives with different employment horizons shape a firm's financial distress risk. These results offer important implications for firms, investors, and regulators.

title: Signaling through Debt Composition: Metric-contingent Finance in AI-agent Firms
affiliations: Hanyang University and Department of Fintech, SKK Business School, Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: Signaling through Debt Composition: Metric-contingent Finance in AI-agent Firms
detail.abstract: Machine-verifiable records let firms borrow against current operations. Financing rules can enter AI controllers directly, changing operations before repayment while ignoring losses elsewhere. We study a firm with private residual asset quality that uses an integrated facility with archived and live metric-contingent terms, plus residual debt. Because investors quote the debt face after observing the package, facility composition becomes a signaling margin. A high-quality firm can chane contract power without changing financing quantity. In a two-state common pool, separation tilts toward live finance if and only if a marginal live dollar collects less where the low type defaults.

title: Inflation, Exchange-rate Volatility and Non-performing Loans in the Banking Sector: Panel Evidence from Ghanaian Commercial Banks

detail.title: Inflation, Exchange-rate Volatility and Non-performing Loans in the Banking Sector: Panel Evidence from Ghanaian Commercial Banks
detail.abstract: When banks cannot recover loans, the entire financial system become inefficient and banks are unable to extend new credit facilities which could lead to stagnated economic growth. This study asks a question: do rising prices and unstable exchange rates translate into bad loans in the banking sector? Using annual panel data for fourteen commercial banks over 2012-2025, the study estimates pooled ordinary least squares, fixed effects and random effects models. The evidence on inflation is unambiguous: as prices rise, borrowers' real income erodes, business cash flows tighten and the incidence of non-performing loans increases. Exchangerate instability tells a more subtle story. Bad loans fall during periods of currency instability, not because borrowers become stronger, but because banks quietly shut the credit door on riskier clients. This defensive lending response may keep balance sheets cleaner in the short run, but it can restrict finance to productive firms when the economy is most fragile. The findings imply that banking stability in Ghana requires disciplined inflation control, stronger exchange-rate risk management and lending frameworks that recognise how macroeconomic stress alters both borrower capacity and bank behaviour.

title: From Transactional Value to the Value-Governance Frontier: Second-Order Economizing in Inter-Organizational Governance

detail.title: From Transactional Value to the Value-Governance Frontier: Second-Order Economizing in Inter-Organizational Governance
detail.abstract: Transaction-cost economics explains governance as a discriminating-alignment problem: match each transaction to the discrete structure-market, hybrid, or hierarchy-that economizes on the costs of exchange. Zajac and Olsen (1993) argued that this costminimizing formulation under-describes inter-organizational relationships, which also create joint value through mutual investment and learning, and proposed a transactionalvalue reorientation. This paper carries that reorientation one step further, from a value to be maximized into an axis to be traded. A transaction operated under a governance structure yields a point in a plane whose axes are value creation and the appropriation hazard to the firm's nexus of intellectual assets; the efficient boundary of the attainable set is a value-governance frontier, and the firm's governance problem is to navigate it. Navigating the frontier is second-order economizing: where first-order economizing maximizes the surplus a transaction creates, second-order economizing governs the appropriation hazard that value creation entails, so that present surplus does not erode the capability base on which future surplus depends. Williamson's discrete modes are recovered as projections of the frontier's operating point; discriminating alignment is the static shadow of a dynamic navigation problem. The paper illustrates the framework with the "reverse acquihire" wave in the artificial-intelligence sector (2024-2026), in which incumbents licensed startups' technology and hired their founders while leaving the corporate shell intact. Read through the frontier, these transactions are not a regulatoryarbitrage innovation but off-frontier operation: by decoupling value capture from governance, the parties reach a jointly dominated point, and the widely reported posttransaction value destruction measures the distance below the frontier. The formal dynamic model underlying the frontier is developed separately (Olsen, 2026a); this paper's contribution is the institutional-economic one-that the transactional-value tradition, extended dynamically, resolves value creation and governance into a single navigable object. In inter-organizational M&A that object is navigated discretely and its misnavigation is observable; in the agent-mediated firm it becomes a boundary recomputed continuously (Olsen, 2026a). The M&A wave is the discrete, legible instance of a governance principle whose continuous form is the emerging economics of the agentic firm.

title:
The Double-slit Correspondence: 
A Five-parameter Structural Framework for Multi-agent AI Governance

detail.title:
The Double-slit Correspondence: 
A Five-parameter Structural Framework for Multi-agent AI Governance
detail.abstract: This paper establishes a five-parameter governance correspondence grounded in the physics of two-slit interference. Each of the five parameters-data gap, agent scope, model independence, observation body, and training data volume-maps exactly to a governance obligation for a specific named executive. The structural lesson: every governance failure mode has a physical equivalent, and every physical parameter has a governance intervention. Part Two of this correspondence (available separately on SSRN) extends the framework to multi-layer cascading architectures.

title: Fiscal Trust or Partisanship? Explaining Resistance to Ghana's E-Levy
affiliations: and University of Cape Coast - Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Fiscal Trust or Partisanship? Explaining Resistance to Ghana's E-Levy
detail.abstract: Ghana's Electronic Transfer Levy (E-Levy) was repealed in April 2025 after three years of sustained public opposition, yet the revenue shortfall it was designed to address remains unresolved, and proposals for a revised version have since been advanced. Existing research on this episode attributes resistance to partisan alignment: supporters of the party that introduced the levy expressed more favourable attitudes toward it than did others. This paper asks whether that partisan account is complete, or whether resistance also reflected a fiscal-legitimacy dimension, specifically distrust in the institutions responsible for collecting and spending tax revenue, that would be expected to persist independently of partisan change. Using Afrobarometer Round 9 survey data from 2,089 Ghanaian respondents, we estimate a nested ordered logistic regression of E-Levy attitudes on party affiliation, perceived corruption among tax officials, and trust in the Ghana Revenue Authority, net of standard demographic controls. Adding the fiscal-legitimacy variables to a partisanship-only model significantly improves fit (LR chisquared = 38.95, p < .001), and trust in the tax authority remains a statistically significant predictor of resistance across every specification tested, including a binary re-coding with region fixed effects and a broader corruption index. Perceived corruption among tax officials, more narrowly defined, is a less stable predictor across specifications. These findings suggest that proposals to redesign the levy around rate or exemption-threshold adjustments alone, without attending to institutional trust, may not adequately address the attitudinal sources of resistance that characterised the original policy. The design is cross-sectional and identifies association, not a causal effect.

title: Accounting for Italy's North-South Divide in Trusting Behaviour: Experimental Evidence from Southern Migrants
affiliations: Masaryk University and PSB Paris School of Business

detail.title: Accounting for Italy's North-South Divide in Trusting Behaviour: Experimental Evidence from Southern Migrants
detail.abstract: Regional economic divides often persist despite free mobility, a puzzle attributed to gaps in trust and cooperation preferences. We study Italy's North-South trust divide to test whether such differences dissolve after migration to a higher-trust region. Using trust-game data from a Northern Italian province, we compare natives, Southern migrants, and other-region migrants: Southern migrants trust 29% less than natives, while other migrants are indistinguishable from them. The gap reflects both more pessimistic beliefs about others' cooperation and lower trustworthiness, with beliefs playing the larger role. Trust does not converge toward natives' levels with time since migration, suggesting persistent cultural traits.

title: The Economics of Lunar Data Centers
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Economics of Lunar Data Centers
detail.abstract: We give an order of magnitude economic assessment of siting compute on the lunar surface, and reach three conclusions. First, the binding constraint is delivered mass, not latency or bandwidth: under a base case of 50 kg per kW of information technology (IT) load, which omits micrometeoroid subdivision, high voltage plasma effects, dust mitigation, seismic margin, and spares for unreplaceable attrition, breakeven against a terrestrial facility requires transport at roughly 300 dollars per kilogram to the lunar surface, against a rocket equation floor of 2,500 to 6,000 and a realized cost near 10 6. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis over wide priors puts the probability that the static comparison favours the Moon at about 0.3 percent, with 87 percent of the variance attributable to transport cost alone. Second, and independently, the project is a race between two exponentials. Writing g for the decline rate of launch cost and δ for the decay rate of margin on installed compute, which combines technological obsolescence at 0.35 with unreplaceable attrition at 0.05, the project is worth building at a finite date only if g > δ, and the stochastic version replaces this with g ≥ δ + σ 2 /2. Conditional on the drift the lifetime construction probability is negligible, but conditioning on a known drift is the wrong exercise: mixing over a prior on g gives a predictive probability below four percent, driven by tail mass above the critical drift rather than by the diffusion. Whether this gets built is a statement about the width of one's belief on launch cost progress and about nothing else. Third, free flying orbital platforms dominate the lunar surface on every margin except shielding mass, and applying the same framework in orbit gives a breakeven within a factor of four of current cost rather than a factor of a thousand. The two lunar markets that survive are compute co-located with lunar industry, and cold archival storage priced off an insurance motive rather than a compute cost comparison.

title: Trade Policy Uncertainty and Small Firm Internationalisation: A Review and Conceptual Framework

detail.title: Trade Policy Uncertainty and Small Firm Internationalisation: A Review and Conceptual Framework
detail.abstract: Trade policy uncertainty has moved from the periphery to the centre of international economics over the past decade, driven by episodes including Brexit, the US-China tariff conflict, and the weakening of multilateral trade governance. While a substantial literature now documents the effects of trade policy uncertainty on aggregate trade flows and large-firm behaviour, its implications for small and medium enterprises remain comparatively under-theorised, despite SMEs' distinctive vulnerability to policy volatility. This paper reviews the theoretical and empirical literature on trade policy uncertainty and firm-level export behaviour, and develops a conceptual framework specifying the mechanisms through which uncertainty affects SME exporters differently from large firms: higher relative sunk costs of market entry and exit, narrower market and product portfolios, constrained access to trade finance and hedging instruments, and higher per-unit information costs of tracking policy developments. The framework generates testable propositions concerning market entry deferral, defensive pricing, and premature market exit, and identifies the policy levers predictability-enhancing commitment mechanisms, SME-targeted trade intelligence, and counter-cyclical trade financemost likely to mitigate uncertainty's dis proportionate burden on smaller exporters. The paper concludes with an agenda for empirical research on SME responses to trade policy volatility.

title: From Crisis to Gains in the Gulf  ?: Decentralized Migration Management, COVID-19 Pandemic Diplomacy, and the Emirati State

detail.title: From Crisis to Gains in the Gulf  ?: Decentralized Migration Management, COVID-19 Pandemic Diplomacy, and the Emirati State

publicationDetails.detailsText:
Forthcoming in Healthcare, Migration, and Politics in the Middle East: The COVID-19 Pandemic in Local Contexts.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03761-9_7

detail.abstract: Despite such central relevance and contributions, mainstream Gulf migration literature has yet to systematically examine and historicize the complex and multiple institutional and political impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on migration management-both at the domestic and international levels-in the Gulf countries. Using the case of the United Arab Emirates (UAE)-a key node of the regional and global migration system in the Gulf and of the Global South-this chapter examines the host states' strategic shift in migration management responses to the COVID-19 pandemic both at the domestic and geopolitical levels. It features threefold arguments: first, despite its state-centric migration management roots, the COVID-19 pandemic has institutionally forced the host states to adopt a decentralized collaborative model of domestic migration management by integrating migrant community organizations into its government crisis approach. Second, the COVID-19 pandemic not only threatened the national interests and capacities of states, but also compelled host states to strategically mobilize a combination of foreign policy coercion and cooperation towards sending states, including those deemed "non-cooperative," to assert their geopolitical power. Third, the COVID-19 pandemic has also strategically triggered host states to reform their domestic migration management, thus enabling them to effectively position their economic strategies (i.e., more liberalized knowledge-based economy) in a post-COVID-19 pandemic scenario. These strategic responses to the COVID-19 pandemic have not only enabled them to project their global humanitarian image and capacity but also mirror the existing regional power politics and asymmetries between host and sending states in the Global South. Methodologically, I employ semi-structured interviews with state and non-state officials and temporary migrant workers, combined with field observation during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2022) in the UAE. I also utilized secondary analysis of local UAE official government policies and newspaper publications to support my empirical findings. Overall, the study contributes to empirical and theoretical discussions on the global politics of migration management by highlighting the role of the global crisis in shaping host states' domestic and foreign policy responses on migration management during the global COVID-19 pandemic period.

title: The Hollowing of Office: Human Sovereignty, Compelled Assent, and the Loss of Discernment When AI Governs in Practice
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Hollowing of Office: Human Sovereignty, Compelled Assent, and the Loss of Discernment When AI Governs in Practice
detail.abstract: This Article identifies an institutional governance failure obscured by conventional human-oversight frameworks: formal authority can remain human while practical governing capacity migrates to artificial-intelligence systems. It calls this pathology the hollowing of office. The Article makes three contributions. First, it distinguishes decision competence from governing competence and explains how epistemically compelled assent and a discernment-atrophy loop can reduce human approval to ceremony. Second, it shifts the unit of analysis from a single human-machine interaction to the office and its surrounding intelligence architecture. The relevant question is whether an institution can still frame problems, contest outputs, intervene, reconstruct decisions, remedy harm, and continue essential functions if the principal system is unavailable. Third, it proposes a proportionate response: a ten-part Minimum Governing Capacity Standard, a Human Discernment Reserve, a Qualified Right of Normative Refusal, tiered obligations, shared assurance capacity, and reciprocal tempo governance for military and financial settings. The argument distinguishes assistive, dependence-producing, and epistemically dominant AI; superintelligence need not be imminent or inevitable. This is a conceptual framework, not a claim that office hollowing is already widespread. Its indicators, research agenda, worked examples, and illustrative statutory provisions are offered for empirical testing and sector-specific adaptation. The central claim is not that humans must outperform advanced AI. Institutions lose legitimacy when they can no longer determine when a system should be resisted, explain why, and act effectively on that judgment.

title: From Housework Traps to Spatialized Poverty: The Changing Landscape of Welfare Dependency and Generalized Trust in South Korea

detail.title: From Housework Traps to Spatialized Poverty: The Changing Landscape of Welfare Dependency and Generalized Trust in South Korea

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study utilized publicly available secondary data from the Korea Welfare Panel Study (KOWEPS). As the dataset contains anonymized data, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines the structural transformation of welfare dependency and social trust in South Korea over a nearly two-decade period (2005 vs 2023). Using household-weighted linear regressions and Firth's penalized logistic models, I demonstrate a profound shift in the 'poverty profile' of the nation. The findings reveal that the 'housework trap'-a unique interaction between domestic labor and psychological distress that predicted welfare entry in 2005-has effectively dissipated. By 2023, welfare status has become increasingly driven by a 'spatialization of poverty'-marked by intense economic pressures in metropolitan Seoul-and a deficit in Positive Psychological Capital (PsyCap). Furthermore, while educational attainment remains a predictor of social trust, its relative influence has diminished, highlighting a persistent 'Education-Trust Paradox' in a highly credentialed society. Crucially, welfare receipt emerged as a significant negative predictor of social trust in 2023, signaling an escalation of latent welfare stigma and institutional alienation. These results suggest that contemporary welfare frameworks in rapidly aging, post-developmental states must transcend traditional monetary transfers. Instead, policy interventions should integrate spatial inequality and psychological resilience to restore social citizenship and mitigate systemic risks.

title: Marginalism and Institutions in the Making of the Economics Profession in Spain, 1900-1959
affiliations: University of Sevilla, Complutense University of Madrid and University of the Balearic Islands - Department of Applied Economics

detail.title: Marginalism and Institutions in the Making of the Economics Profession in Spain, 1900-1959
detail.abstract: This article examines how economists emerged as a distinct professional community in Spain between the early twentieth century and the Stabilization Plan of 1959. It argues that the historical significance of marginalism lay not in establishing a unified economic doctrine but in providing the common analytical language through which economists forged a shared professional identity. By distinguishing economists from competing expert communities, this methodological framework strengthened their claims to scientific authority and technical competence. Yet marginalism alone does not explain the growing political influence of economists. Combining intellectual history, institutional analysis, and social network analysis, the article shows that the consolidation of the profession also depended upon the gradual construction of an institutional and social network linking universities, financial institutions, government ministries, research institutes, specialist journals, and international organizations. Together, these institutions transformed a shared methodological language into professional authority and professional authority into political and administrative influence. The Stabilization Plan of 1959 therefore appears less as the starting point of Spain's technocratic transformation than as the culmination of a longer process through which economists became one of the Franco regime's principal expert communities..

title: Double Jeopardy: The Climate and Fiscal Space Crises in Small Island Developing States
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Double Jeopardy: The Climate and Fiscal Space Crises in Small Island Developing States
detail.abstract: The fiscal space crisis overlaps with the climate crisis in developing countries, complicating efforts to achieve sustainable development goals, especially in small island developing states (SIDS). This paper examines the impact of a year of extreme weather events on fiscal balance and investment in small island states. The paper utilizes a panel dataset of 26 countries across three regions (the Caribbean, the Pacific, and Atlantic, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean and South China Sea, AIMS) from 1990 to 2023. It employs a dynamic event study that accounts for heterogeneous treatment effects. The results show that extreme weather events impact the fiscal space of SIDS. In the treatment year, extreme weather events negatively impact fiscal balance and persist in post-treatment years. Net lending and borrowing exhibit similar pattern to fiscal balance, albeit with slightly greater elasticity, as indicated by the coefficients. This suggests that after an extreme weather event, governments of small island states tend to increase public borrowing to offset losses and meet budgetary needs, including the repair of damaged infrastructure, as borrowing costs rise. The revenue loss is attributable to declines in tax revenue, exports, and primary income. The results also show that weather shocks have a statistically significant negative impact on gross fixed capital formation and education spending.

title: The Skeleton Key: Borrowed Urgency, Unpredicated Child Exploitation Suspicion, and the Cost No Plaintiff Can Recover

detail.title: The Skeleton Key: Borrowed Urgency, Unpredicated Child Exploitation Suspicion, and the Cost No Plaintiff Can Recover
detail.abstract: A federal officer who wants to search a traveler's phone at the border needs no warrant, no probable cause, and in the Eleventh Circuit no suspicion of any kind. Yet officers still give reasons, and the reason they give is not doctrinally idle. This article examines what happens when the reason given is child sexual exploitation and the record contains no predicate for it. The immediate cost falls on the traveler and is litigated in the ordinary way, through suppression. A second cost falls on a population that will never appear in the caption. Every unpredicated invocation of child exploitation as a search rationale spends down the credibility of the same assertion when it is made with a predicate, teaches the public to hear the phrase as an access request rather than an allegation, and supplies the strongest available argument to platforms resisting genuine child protection obligations. That cost is real, it is attributable, and no doctrine can reach it. Standing runs to the searched party, suppression compensates the searched party, and pretext analysis after Whren declines to examine subjective motive at all. The article traces the border search regime and its own internal suspicion floor, identifies why child exploitation is the optimal pretext under that regime, locates the structural blindness in standing and remedy rather than in judicial indifference, and proposes a contemporaneous articulation requirement calibrated to the one protection the agency already imposes on itself.

title: The Latent: Finite Sufficient Representations of Smooth Systems

detail.title: The Latent: Finite Sufficient Representations of Smooth Systems
detail.abstract:
We define the Latent of a smooth system as the basis-free element of a graded Hilbert tensor algebra that completely characterizes the system's distributional, dynamic, and functional properties. The paper develops 35 theorems and propositions and includes formal verification in Lean 4 and the Platonic kernel.

title: Macroeconomic Effects and Labor Market Reallocation under the EU Digital Product Passport Mandate An Integrated Heterogeneous Firms, Porter, Task Based, and Search Matching Analysis

detail.title: Macroeconomic Effects and Labor Market Reallocation under the EU Digital Product Passport Mandate An Integrated Heterogeneous Firms, Porter, Task Based, and Search Matching Analysis
