title: Artificial Intelligence in Energy Risk Underwriting
affiliations: MGIMO and

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Energy Risk Underwriting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) - Master's Student Sogaz (Russian Insurance Company) - Worker

publicationDetails.detailsText: The 14th Annual International Scientific and Practical Conference "Insurance AI: A New Era in Global Insurance?", MGIMO, 2025

detail.abstract: The ongoing transformation of the insurance industry through artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most significant developments of recent years. Now AI is permeating a broad range of business processes: from dynamic underwriting to automated claims handling. However, in energy risk insurance this shift faces substantial constraints. The sector's defining characteristics-highly distinctive features of each asset, considerable insured values, and the inherent unpredictability of the risks involved-demand not only computational accuracy, but also profound professional judgment. This paper advances the thesis that, in the context of energy insurance, AI should be considered solely as a support tool-one that augments, yet in no way supplants, the underwriter's professional expertise.

title: Who Backs Women? Business Angels' Traits and Investment in Female Entrepreneurship
affiliations: University of Piemonte Orientale - Department of Economics and Business Studies, , Universita Del Piemonte Orientale and

detail.title: Who Backs Women? Business Angels' Traits and Investment in Female Entrepreneurship

declarations.funderStatement: The data used in this study were collected within the BAC4SHC project ("Business Angels and Crowd investors for startups' human capital"), which has received funding from the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (Staff Exchanges), grant agreement No 101129958 (HORIZON-MSCA-2022-SE-01-01).

detail.abstract: Despite growing scholarly attention to gender disparities in entrepreneurial finance, existing research has predominantly focused on venture-level characteristics to explain the funding gap faced by women-led ventures. How investor-side traits relate to this gap remains an open and underexplored question. Drawing on a unique survey dataset of 84 business angels (BAs) operating across Italy, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, this study provides pioneering evidence on the associations between BAs' personal characteristics, human capital, investment practices, and their exposure to women-led ventures. We identify consistent empirical associations: membership in an angel network and co-investment alongside venture capital funds are each positively related to greater exposure to female entrepreneurship. These associations remain stable across alternative model specifications. Taken together, our findings shift the analytical lens from the demand side to the supply side of the angel market and have direct implications for angel network design, investor training, and policy initiatives aimed at broadening women entrepreneurs' access to early-stage capital.

title: Who Provides It Matters: Source Characteristics and Trust in Online Information
affiliations: , University of Mannheim - Department of Economics and University of Mannheim - Department of Economics

detail.title: Who Provides It Matters: Source Characteristics and Trust in Online Information
detail.abstract: We study how observable characteristics of information sources shape individuals' evaluations of their content. In an online experiment, we vary source characteristics while holding content constant. We find that disclosing these characteristics leaves both the content's perceived accuracy and the willingness to share it largely unaffected but substantially shapes trust in the source. Highly educated sources are trusted more; disclosing low education, popularity, and Republican affiliation each reduces trust. Participants sort across sources based on observable characteristics even before seeing any content, suggesting that source cues serve as credibility signals that influence who is trusted and heard.

title: Protracted Processes and the Timing of Disclosure After the Listing Act

detail.title: Protracted Processes and the Timing of Disclosure After the Listing Act
detail.abstract: The Listing Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2809) and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/789 have recast the timing o fissuers’ disclosure under Article 17 MAR: the prohibition of insider dealing continues to attach to inside information as soon as it arises, while the duty to disclose is, for protracted processes, postponed to the final event listed — non-exhaustively — in Annex I to the Delegated Regulation, with a new confidentiality duty covering the intermediate phase. Drawing on the Level 2 record, from ESMA’s consultation to the adopted text, the paper defends an inclusive construction of the notion of protracted process — a participation test rather than a control test — under which any process in which the issuer performs at least some of the steps is disclosed at its final event, including processes whose decisive step lies with an authority, a court or a counterparty. The case for that construction is exegetical and functional alike, since the contrary reading would reintroduce the early disclosure of immature information that the reform sought to avoid. The paper then examines the immediate-disclosure regime of profit warnings and earnings surprises, distinguishing its textually secure ground from its inferential extensions; reads the thirty-five entries of Annex I as a repertoire of formal disclosure anchors available for analogical reasoning; reconstructs the recast relationship between the delay of disclosure and the treatment of intermediate steps; and identifies in the attribution of knowledge to the issuer — now pending before the Court of Justice — the major question that the reform leaves open.

title: Bayesian Bootstrap Ensembles for Low-Rank Causal Discovery

detail.title: Bayesian Bootstrap Ensembles for Low-Rank Causal Discovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses exclusively publicly available, de-identiffed datasets.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no speciffc grant from any funding agency. Computing resources were purchased by the author personally.

detail.abstract: Objective: Differentiable causal discovery methods produce point estimates of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) but lack uncertainty quantification. Existing uncertainty-aware methods are limited to d ≤ 50 due to O(d 3) complexity, while genomic studies routinely profile d ≥ 500 genes. We develop a Bayesian bootstrap ensemble of low-rank models to produce posterior edge probabilities under a Dirichlet process prior (Rubin 1981). Results: Low-rank factorization (W = U V ⊤ , r ≪ d) reduces the DAG constraint from O(d 3) to O(dr 2). Dirichlet-weighted Bayesian bootstrap across 20-50 training runs yields ensemble distributions over the adjacency matrix, outperforming standard resampling-based bootstrap on difficult configurations: at d = 50, standard bootstrap detects zero edges (F1 = 0.000) while the Bayesian bootstrap recovers edges (F1 = 0.025); at d = 200, the Bayesian bootstrap more than doubles F1 (0.080 vs. 0.034; Supplementary Table S4). On synthetic Erdős-Rényi DAGs (d = 30-500), expected calibration error (ECE) decreases from 0.036 at d = 30 (comparable to DiBS at 0.038) to 0.003 at d = 500, where DiBS is inapplicable. On TCGA BRCA expression data (d = 500, n = 1,218), the 21 edges with posterior probability exceeding baseline (P > 0.1, out of 250,000 candidates) achieve 71.4% combined STRING protein-protein interaction validation precision (vs. 10.6% baseline)-a 6.7-fold enrichment.

title: First Impressions Matter: The Lasting Impact of Slanted Media on Attitudes
affiliations: , University of Mannheim - Department of Economics and University of Verona - Department of Economics

detail.title: First Impressions Matter: The Lasting Impact of Slanted Media on Attitudes
detail.abstract: We investigate how slanted articles influence attitudes. We conducted a field experiment in which university students were randomly assigned to different treatments, reading news articles with either a positive or negative slant on both familiar and novel topics over four weeks. We collected students' attitudes weekly and conducted a follow-up survey four weeks after the experiment ended. We find that: a) slanted information significantly shifts attitudes in the intended direction; b) the effect is more substantial for novel topics; c) the first impression about a novel topic shapes attitudes; d) the change in attitudes persists over time. Our findings highlight that media are more effective at shaping initial attitudes than at altering pre-existing ones. Thus, our results show the importance of providing timely information in the early stages of public discourse.

title: A Global Geometric Transformation for Critical Transition Detection in Complex Financial Systems
affiliations: Dublin City University,  and Dublin City University Business School

detail.title: A Global Geometric Transformation for Critical Transition Detection in Complex Financial Systems
detail.abstract: A geometric framework for analyzing high-dimensional financial systems under noise is introduced. Unlike traditional econometric methods that reduce noise through smoothing, this new approach works directly on relational geometric representations without needing to remove noise. Each market state is shown as a relational geometric instance, defined by pairwise interactions among financial variables. This transforms temporal financial data into a flexible geometric form, reflecting changes in the relationships within the financial system. The proposed model does not assume stationarity, ergodicity, linearity, or any specific distribution form. By integrating local relational deviations on a global scale, the framework reduces inconsistent disturbances(noise) while maintaining coherent structural changes related to market instability. A global dataset of equity indices from major financial regions, covering the years 2005 to 2021, demonstrates that several significant financial disruptions align with recognizable geometric deformation patterns. This framework forms a new link between geometric representation theory and financial system analysis.

title:
The AI Zettelkasten: An Intermediate Memory for the Literature of a Sociological Subfield 
A Field Report and How-To
affiliations: German Youth Institute DJI

detail.title:
The AI Zettelkasten: An Intermediate Memory for the Literature of a Sociological Subfield 
A Field Report and How-To
detail.abstract: Debates in computational social science (CSS) tend to focus on data acquisition and algorithmic analysis. What remains underexposed is the question of how to organize the systematic synthesis of research literatures that are expanding rapidly, driven by publication pressure, cumulative dissertation formats, and journal proliferation - and to do so in a way that keeps them machine-processable and hermeneutically accessible at the same time. This paper presents an infrastructure that operates at the intersection of CSS and classical literature work within a sociological subfield. Its core is an Obsidian vault holding several hundred structured Markdown summaries of scientific publications - AI-generated, human-annotated and corrected, and immediately readable - interconnected through a curated taxonomy and linked back to the original sources. The Markdown files function as a rapidly readable intermediate memory that makes every interpretive step visible, checkable, and correctable; in a sample audit reported below, fabricated content is roughly three times rarer than in bulk-generated summaries, and the errors that remain become locatable. This intermediate memory serves human researchers just as much as powerful, locally orchestrated AI agents (here: Claude Opus via Claude Code). Markdown, LaTeX/Beamer, and R form a token-economical ecosystem: summaries compress the underlying PDFs by a factor of five to ten, and plain-text artifacts avoid the tooling friction of binary formats. The entire workflow unfolds in a text-based working environment in which Claude Code operates as an executing compiler: multiple specialized agents read PDFs, produce Markdown summaries, derive analytic methods, implement them in R, execute the code, interpret the results, and compile presentations and papers in LaTeX. Writing this report doubled as the system's most rigorous audit to date: the manuscript's adversarial review exposed counting bugs and documentation lag, and the same-day fixes are part of the result. The paper addresses three tensions: (1) automated text processing versus hermeneutic interpretation; (2) the connection to multivariate statistics, since highly complex R code is generated directly from reading methods papers; (3) the epistemological question of what it means when AI agents step in as an intermediary between primary source and researcher. The paper thereby sketches a how-to for an AI-assisted multi-agent workflow of (sociological) knowledge production whose potential ultimately scales with the rapidly growing capabilities of AI systems. It closes on a constraint that reaches beyond any single setup: such a memory can hold only what may lawfully enter it, so literature that cannot be legally processed risks slipping below the threshold of perception - which makes permissive text-and-data-mining terms a question of visibility, not only of access.

title: Homeownership Access of French Households after the Inflation Shock

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on anonymized banking data and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. detail.abstract: This paper documents the reorganization of the mortgage-lending function of a French cooperative bank following the European Central Bank tightening initiated in July 2022. The original sample comprises 700 mortgage files drawn from the Caisse d'Épargne Côte d'Azur portfolio (352 in 2021, 348 in 2023), reduced to 696 observations for inference. Three methods are combined: OLS regression with HC3 standard errors, principal component analysis, and a pooled regression with year-by-variable interactions completed by a Chow test. The Chow test rejects the null of identical allocation functions at F(7, 682) = 7.31 (p = 1.78 × 10 ⁸). The break localizes on two variables. The standardized coefficient on Monthly ⁻ Salary rises from +0.413 to +0.761 (interaction +0.349; p = 0.051). The coefficient on Loan Maturity falls from +0.405 to +0.201 (interaction-0.204; p = 0.001). The Maturity result is robust to a Bonferroni correction across six tests; the Salary result remains at the edge of conventional significance. The other determinants-Age, Debt-to-Income, Marital Status, Gross Real-Estate Wealth-do not evolve significantly. We interpret this shift as the mechanical consequence of saturated French macroprudential levers, which forces the bank to reallocate adjustment onto ex ante salary-based screening. To our knowledge, this is the first econometric formalization of such a shift at the scale of a single French bank, with a structural break test and year-by-variable interactions. The theoretical reading draws on the bank-lending channel (Bernanke and Gertler, 1995) extended by the macroprudential framework. We discuss implications for regulators, banks, and the homeownership access of modest households.

title:
A Practical Constitution Under Arms
State Judaism, Military Citizenship, and Conditional Obedience in the Israel Defense Forces

detail.title:
A Practical Constitution Under Arms
State Judaism, Military Citizenship, and Conditional Obedience in the Israel Defense Forces
detail.abstract: In Israel, the conflict between religion and state reaches its most intense institutional form inside the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). Israel is neither a theocracy nor a secular state in any strict sense. It is a Jewish nation-state whose architecture combines parliamentary sovereignty, partial rabbinic authority, militarized citizenship, territorial nationalism, and a coalition system that turns religious parties into veto players. Within that frame the army is not merely a defense organization. It also distributes belonging, prestige, duties, and access to resources; it incorporates religious authorities; it administers territories charged with biblical meaning; and it converts abstract disputes over national identity into concrete problems of command and obedience. The article reconstructs that architecture from the status quo letter of 1947, the founding ambiguity of the Declaration of Independence, the rabbinical jurisdiction over marriage and divorce established in 1953, and the 2018 Basic Law on Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People. It then analyzes the Military Rabbinate, the hesder yeshivot, the religious premilitary academies, the conflicts over gender, the dispute over the settlements, and the prolonged crisis of haredi conscription. The argument culminates in an interpretation of the current conjuncture as a crisis of mamlachtiyut: the Ben-Gurionist principle that subordinates sectoral loyalties to state authority. That crisis advances from three different directions: the haredi world, which asserts Torah study against military service; national-religious sectors, which may condition obedience when the state acts against territories held to be sacred; and secularliberal sectors, which during the judicial crisis of 2023 set limits on voluntary service in defense of the constitutional order. The war that began on October 7, 2023 did not resolve those tensions. It made them more urgent and more visible, and it left them harder to administer.

title: Structural Convergence in Gacha Mechanism Design: An Empirical Taxonomy of Stochastic Reward Systems Against Optimal-Pricing Theory

detail.title: Structural Convergence in Gacha Mechanism Design: An Empirical Taxonomy of Stochastic Reward Systems Against Optimal-Pricing Theory
detail.abstract: Gacha monetization systems—stochastic reward mechanisms through which players purchase randomized draws for virtual items—mediate tens of billions of dollars of annual revenue, yet their designs have evolved largely by industry intuition. Recent mechanism-design theory (Gan, 2022) proves that, facing buyers with cumulative-prospect-theory preferences, a revenue maximizing seller’s optimal dynamic mechanism is closely approximated by a hard pity system that truncates the expenditure tail. This theory has so far been validated against only two games. This paper conducts the first systematic empirical test of the prediction across the industry. We formalize each deployed mechanism as a tuple M = ({pn}, N, q, G, S) of hazard schedule, hard-pity threshold, featured share, guarantee automaton, and spark threshold, and encode 25 mechanisms spanning Chinese, Japanese, and Korean publishers from 2015–2024. For each mechanism we compute the exact distribution of expenditure to a targeted item by dynamic programming, and evaluate each distribution under a Tversky–Kahneman (1992) buyer to obtain a certainty-equivalent behavioral markup µ = CE/E[T]. Five findings emerge. First, 23/25 deployed mechanisms achieve µ < 1, clustered in 0.85–0.98; the two exceptions are structurally distinguished, with pre-2022 Fate/Grand Order (µ = 1.068) being the sole unbounded-tail mechanism and retrofitted with a guarantee in 2022 (µ = 0.954)—a within title natural experiment supporting the theory. Second, a random-mechanism baseline (3,000 draws from a plausible commercial prior) achieves µ < 1 at rate 81% overall and 86% among bounded mechanisms, so the deployed sample’s 92% share is not statistically dramatic against a mechanism-space baseline (p = 0.12); the industry’s decisive convergence is on boundedness itself, not on cross-sectional optimality among bounded designs. Third, component ablation identifies tail truncation—hard pity or spark—as the causal driver of µ < 1: removing tail truncation raises µ across seven of eight tested mechanisms, in every case where truncation is the binding constraint. Fourth, sensitivity analysis proves µ is invariant to the loss-aversion parameter λ, while the value-function curvature β dominates: at β = 1 six mechanisms cross µ = 1, isolating the specific psychological mechanism the theory relies on. Fifth, the aggregate time trend in µ is directionally consistent with convergence (−0.0034/year) but not significant (p = 0.39, n = 25). We interpret the industry as having converged structurally to the principle—randomize, but truncate the tail—rather than to a common cross-sectional point, and we provide first theoretical treatments of two industry features absent from Gan’s model: identity-level “coinflip” guarantees as a price-discrimination interpretation, and strategic hazard obfuscation as a conjectured signaling device.

title: Federalism In Transition: State-Wise Divergence and Implementation Gaps Under the Osh Code, 2020

detail.title: Federalism In Transition: State-Wise Divergence and Implementation Gaps Under the Osh Code, 2020
detail.abstract: The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 consolidates thirteen central labour statutes into a single framework, and was finally brought into force on 21 November 2025 five years after its enactment. This paper examines the gap between the Code’s promise of a unified national safety regime and the reality of its staggered, state-dependent rollout. While most states notified their rules years in advance, others, including West Bengal, have yet to fully do so, leaving establishments to operate under overlapping and sometimes contradictory legal regimes during the transition. Drawing on the Code, the Central Rules of 2026, official notifications, and Ministry of Labour clarifications, this paper argues that India’s federal structure with labour on the Concurrent List has produced exactly the fragmentation the Code sought to eliminate, and proposes measures to close this gap.

title: From Point Sensors to Spatial Hazard Interpretation in Underground Coal Mining: A Critical Review of Longwall Monitoring, Validation and Deployment Readiness
affiliations: , University of New South Wales (UNSW), University of Southern Queensland and University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: From Point Sensors to Spatial Hazard Interpretation in Underground Coal Mining: A Critical Review of Longwall Monitoring, Validation and Deployment Readiness
detail.abstract: An active longwall face is a large, continuously advancing underground area where high-volume coal extraction takes place. Workers operate alongside heavy machinery under hazardous conditions that may include methane accumulation, airborne coal dust, unstable ground and restricted visibility. Established monitoring systems provide essential measurements of gas concentrations, dust exposure, ground behaviour, equipment states and worker locations. However, these measurements are often tied to individual sensors or monitored points, which limits their ability to explain how hazards develop across the surrounding scene. This review examines how safety monitoring at active longwall faces can move from isolated measurements toward more interpretable spatial evidence. It reviews three sensing streams: non-visual monitoring, visual sensing and three-dimensional sensing, across atmospheric, ground-control and personnel-machine interaction hazards. The review shows that non-visual monitoring remains the mature safety backbone of longwall operations, while visual and 3D methods can extend this evidence with information on workers, equipment, smoke, heat, distance, clearance, deformation and spatial relationships. It further shows that deployment is shaped not only by sensing performance, but also by hazardous-area protection, communication reliability, environmental robustness and regulatory acceptance. At the same time, available validation datasets remain limited, task-specific and rarely representative of active longwall environments. The review therefore identifies a need for stronger validation pathways that combine controlled underground trials, realistic simulations, and shared benchmark datasets. It also outlines future research directions for protected bandwidth-aware monitoring systems that combine established sensor readings with visual and geometric evidence to support spatially interpretable hazard assessment.

title: Deaccumulation in India: The Role of Equity, Debt and Annuities in Retirement Income
affiliations: Samasthiti Advisors and

detail.title: Deaccumulation in India: The Role of Equity, Debt and Annuities in Retirement Income
detail.abstract: Framework: We adopt a partial annuitisation framework in which a fraction of the retirement corpus is used to purchase an immediate life annuity, while the remainder is retained in a self-managed portfolio. Using a bootstrap Monte Carlo approach with Indian equity, debt and inflation data, we simulate retirement paths across four portfolio allocations, three annuitisation levels (0, 20 and 40 per cent) and four annuity payout rates (6, 7, 8 and 9 per cent). We also compute money's worth ratios (MWRs) for immediate annuity products, using a Nelson-Siegel government securities (G-sec) yield curve and two Indian mortality tables, based on annuity quotes collected in May 2026. Findings: First, the effect of partial annuitisation on portfolio failure rates depends critically on the annuity payout rate. At payout rates of 6-7 per cent, annuitisation raises failure rates relative to a fully self-managed portfolio. At approximately 8 per cent, its effect is broadly neutral and depends on the withdrawal rate. At 9 per cent, annuitisation consistently reduces failure rates across all portfolio types. Second, products with return of purchase price (with ROP) are priced close to actuarial fairness across all ages, with MWRs of 0.92-0.98, and offer near-fair-value longevity protection with capital recovery. Third, product selection and the timing of annuitisation matter substantially. The choice between with-ROP and without-ROP products, and the age at which an annuity is purchased, can shift a subscriber from the harmful regime to the neutral or beneficial regime. Implications: Annuity payout rates, product type, withdrawal rates and annuitisation timing must be considered jointly in retirement planning. At retirement age 60, prevailing without-ROP rates place retirees in the neutral-to-harmful regime. Subscribers who defer annuitisation to age 70 or beyond, or select without-ROP products whose payout rates clear the 8 per cent threshold, may obtain longevity protection without sacrificing portfolio sustainability.

title: Economic Resistance of the Population and the Two-Loop Model of Deterrence

detail.title: Economic Resistance of the Population and the Two-Loop Model of Deterrence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it is based exclusively on theoretical analysis and publicly available information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper forms part of the Internal Resistance series within the broader research program on Economic Guarantees of Security (EGS). It develops the concept of domestic economic resistance by the population as an integral, critical, and measurable component of deterring aggressive state policy. The paper argues that aggression can be constrained not only from outside the potential aggressor state, but also from within it. The study presents a two-loop model of deterrence that links international economic measures with the internal resistance of economic agents. It also examines the principal forms of economic resistance by the population as a key factor affecting domestic stability. Traditional approaches to deterrence rely primarily on external military, economic, financial, and political instruments. By contrast, the proposed approach focuses on transmitting the expected and actual consequences of aggressive policy into the domestic socioeconomic structure of the state. In the context of the further development of the Economic Guarantees of Security framework, the paper concludes that a comprehensive system for stabilizing political equilibria must combine external economic, financial, and political instruments with the economic resistance of the population, thereby making aggression both costly and internally unacceptable. In our previous studies, the principal elements of the EGS system—threats of punishment for aggression and incentives for peaceful settlement— were addressed directly to state leaders. The main contribution of the present paper is a preliminary design of a two-loop model of economic deterrence, in which international measures influence the leadership of a potential aggressor state not only directly, but also indirectly, by changing the expectations of economic participants and intensifying internal resistance. The central conclusion is that military aggression may be prevented not only through external sanctions, but also through the domestic economic reactions of the population.

reference: Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, volume 10, issue 1, 2016[10.1002/sej.1210]
title: The Equilibrating and Disequilibrating Effects of Entrepreneurship: Revisiting the Central Premises
affiliations: University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business and York University

detail.title: The Equilibrating and Disequilibrating Effects of Entrepreneurship: Revisiting the Central Premises

publicationDetails.detailsText: Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, volume 10, issue 1, 2016[10.1002/sej.1210]

detail.abstract: We review existing theoretical propositions on the equilibrating and disequilibrating effects of entrepreneurship in the market process. We then introduce a game theoretical model of the market process and employ computer simulation to analyze it through time. The formal analysis suggests that entrepreneurship as the creation of new opportunities may not always be disequilibrating, and entrepreneurship as the discovery and exploitation of existing opportunities may not always be equilibrating. We identify specific conditions that produce counterexamples to the generic equilibration and disequilibration propositions previously considered to be the central premises of entrepreneurship research. Managerial summary Many entrepreneurs advance society by building businesses around creative new ideas. Yet, other entrepreneurs start businesses by discovering opportunities to profit without necessarily innovative ideas. In reality, most entrepreneurship involves both creation and discovery. We run computer simulations of a small hypothetical economy to analyze the impact of creation and discovery actions on the extent to which the economy contains unexploited opportunities at any given time. Our results largely support previous ideas on how entrepreneurs help clear the markets by discovering opportunities or how innovations disrupt the market through creative destruction. Our results also highlight ways in which these ideas may be oversimplified and may have boundary conditions.

title: Dual-segmented Rank-referenced Discounting (DSRD) to transform Asking Price into a Transaction-price Proxy in Opaque Real Estate Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dual-segmented Rank-referenced Discounting (DSRD) to transform Asking Price into a Transaction-price Proxy in Opaque Real Estate Markets
detail.abstract: When valuing property using the market approach, asking prices often serve as the primary data source due to the limited availability of reliable transaction data. However, asking prices do not always reflect fair market value, thus requiring an adjustment in the form of a discount before being used as a transaction-price proxy and valuation anchor. This research introduces Dual-Segmented Rank-Referenced Discounting (DSRD), an innovative quantitative model that asymmetrically splits residuals into two market-behaviour domains: the underpriced side (negative) and the overpriced side (positive). Through rank-based variable transformation and segmented regression, DSRD isolates natural discount margins non-symmetrically without outlier distortion or cancelling effects. The Cost Frontier model in Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) posits that costs contain both noise and inefficiency. DSRD adapts this modelling logic by treating discounts as a form of inefficiency stemming from information asymmetry in the market, where the actual magnitude depends on literacy and knowledge regarding assets and market dynamics. The primary focus of DSRD is the proportional separation of random market variance from the influence of information asymmetry, rather than efficiency ranking as in SFA. Unlike SFA, DSRD is dual-sided, entirely data-driven without restrictive parametric distribution assumptions, and guarantees computational stability and convergence without requiring iterative optimisation. Regression analysis of residual data from hedonic price modelling of residential properties in an administrative area of Banten Province demonstrates the feasibility of DSRD as a foundation for determining negotiation margins and establishing a transaction-price proxy.

title: Energy Policy, Institutional Quality, and The Political Economy of Solar Energy Deployment in West Africa
affiliations: Institut National Polytechnique Félix Houphouët-Boigny (INP-HB)

detail.title: Energy Policy, Institutional Quality, and The Political Economy of Solar Energy Deployment in West Africa
detail.abstract: West Africa possesses one of the most favorable solar resource endowments in the world global horizontal irradiation of 1,800-2,500 kWh/m²/year across the Sahelian belt, roughly twice the yield of Germany, historically the world's largest solar market yet solar photovoltaics supplied barely 1% of installed regional generation capacity as of 2023. This paper investigates why a region with abundant, increasingly cheap renewable resources and an elaborate regional institutional architecture (ECOWAS, the West African Power Pool, the ECOWAS Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency, and the ECOWAS Regional Electricity Regulatory Authority) continues to deploy solar capacity far below its technical and economic potential. Using a structured comparative case study of four contiguous but institutionally divergent states Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Mali, and Niger the paper combines institutional analysis, comparative regulatory scoring (the ERERA Electricity Regulatory Index), levelized cost of energy (LCOE) comparison, and a blended-finance mapping of eleven multilateral, bilateral, and climate-dedicated financing institutions. The analysis shows that national regulatory quality, not resource endowment or capital availability, is the principal variable mediating the translation of regional policy commitments into installed capacity: Côte d'Ivoire's mature public-private concession framework (ERI score 6.8/10) has attracted a solar pipeline exceeding 600 MW, while the three Sahelian states, despite superior irradiation, remain dependent on public and concessional finance because of structurally insolvent offtakers (ERI scores of 3.5-4.2/10). The paper develops a four-tier conceptual framework linking regional norms, blended financing architecture, national regulatory mediation, and project-level outcomes, and uses it to interpret two contrasting 2030-2050 energy scenarios. It concludes with differentiated policy recommendations for governments, regional and multilateral institutions, and private investors, and situates these findings within energy transition theory, institutional economics, and the sustainable development goals. The paper argues that closing the region's electrification gap is primarily a governance and institutional-risk challenge rather than a technological or resource constraint.

title: Did the Narrative Break? Designed versus Imposed Shocks in ECB Rhetoric over Three Decades
affiliations: Central Bank of Armenia

detail.title: Did the Narrative Break? Designed versus Imposed Shocks in ECB Rhetoric over Three Decades

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official position of the Central Bank of Armenia.

detail.abstract: Does central bank communication undergo systematic reorientation in the wake of events that fundamentally redefine its institutional environment? This paper traces the evolution of seven economic policy themes across three decades of European Central Bank (ECB) speeches, conceptualizing six major real-economy shocks—the 2008 financial crisis, the 2012 banking union decision, the 2021 digital euro and climate action plans, and the 2022 geopolitical conflict alongside its attendant inflation surge—as sequentially staggered treatments. Applying difference-in-differences estimators specifically calibrated for non-simultaneous treatment adoption, I uncover a pronounced rhetorical schism: endogenous initiatives championed by the ECB attract progressively warmer linguistic sentiment over time, whereas exogenous shocks imposed upon the institution elicit a discernibly colder discursive response. Although this bifurcation withstands a stringent battery of robustness checks, not every pairwise comparison fully satisfies the requisite identification diagnostics.

title: On the Empirical Failure of the Black-Scholes Option Pricing Equation: A Quantitative Assessment of Its Structural Assumptions Against Observed Market Behavior

detail.title: On the Empirical Failure of the Black-Scholes Option Pricing Equation: A Quantitative Assessment of Its Structural Assumptions Against Observed Market Behavior
detail.abstract: The Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) partial differential equation is one of the most cited results in mathematical finance, and its derivation from geometric Brownian motion (GBM) and a continuously-hedged, no-arbitrage portfolio is internally rigorous. This paper does not dispute the mathematics of the derivation; instead, it evaluates the model as an empirical proposition by systematically testing the validity of its five foundational assumptions against documented market data and reproducible simulation: (1) constant, known volatility; (2) lognormally distributed, continuous asset returns; (3) frictionless, continuous trading; (4) constant risk-free rates with no dividends; and (5) the absence of price jumps. For each assumption we present quantitative evidence of violation, including the post-1987 implied-volatility skew, the leptokurtosis and negative skewness of index return distributions, the near-zero probability the model assigns to observed crash events, GARCHtype volatility clustering, Monte Carlo evidence on residual delta-hedging risk under discrete rebalancing, and jump-diffusion path behavior. We find that each assumption is empirically rejected, that the violations are economically material (not merely statistically significant), and that these failures jointly explain systematic Black-Scholes mispricing documented in the literature, particularly the underpricing of out-of-the-money index puts by an average of 8.21 implied-volatility points relative to at-the-money options since 1987. We conclude that Black-Scholes functions today primarily as a quoting convention and a pedagogical benchmark rather than a literal description of price dynamics, and we summarize the extensions (local volatility, stochastic volatility, jump-diffusion, and transaction-cost-aware hedging) that the industry has adopted in its place.

title: An Open Firm-Level Microsimulation for UK VAT Threshold Policy Analysis

detail.title: An Open Firm-Level Microsimulation for UK VAT Threshold Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: I present an open firm-level microsimulation for transparent, conditional costing of UK VAT registration-threshold reforms. The model generates a weighted accounting population from public aggregates; it does not recover administrative microdata or firm behaviour. On a common 2023-24 baseline, I apply level, shape (a taper), and rate (a reduced-rate band) scenarios and report their mechanical revenue effects. I characterise the notch by its modelimplied dominated region-a £21,250 band above the £85,000 threshold-and show how each schedule changes it. Intensive-margin results are sensitivity exercises conditional on a regionconfined response model and assumed elasticities; the extensive margin is not identified. The near-threshold shape is target-inherited, and specification diagnostics show that the synthetic data cannot support bunching inference. The exercise therefore supplies reproducible policy scenarios and a general warning: calibrated synthetic data cannot create behavioural or sub-band fiscal information absent from their targets and maintained assumptions.

title: Lessons from Romaniaʼs EU Accession for Todayʼs Candidate States
affiliations: Romanian Academy - Romanian Academy, Alpha Bank Romania and Cardiff Business School

detail.title: Lessons from Romaniaʼs EU Accession for Todayʼs Candidate States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare in this regard
declarations.funderStatement: Nobody funded

detail.abstract: Romaniaʼs EU accession in 2007, after a decade of externally anchored reform, offers an instructive case for todayʼs enlargement candidates. This paper examines the pre-accession periodʼs reform achievements and their limits, the post-accession reversal driven by moral hazard and political economy, and sectoral outcomes across energy, information technology, public administration, and judicial reform. It then situates Romaniaʼs macro-structural trajectory — consumption-led convergence, twin deficits, and a narrowing fiscal corridor — within the broader convergence debate. Five lessons emerge for current candidates: conditionality is powerful but time-limited; fiscal institutions matter more than fiscal targets; absorption capacity is a binding constraint that must be built pre-accession; post-accession boom-bust dynamics are predictable and require a pre-emptive policy; and honest political narratives about the benefits and costs of reforms are a precondition for durable change.

title: Using Pre-trends for Inference in Difference-in-Differences
affiliations: SciencesPo - Sciences Po - Department of Economics

detail.title: Using Pre-trends for Inference in Difference-in-Differences
detail.abstract: Difference-in-differences (DID) are sometimes estimated with many pre-treatment periods. In such settings, the observed pre-treatment outcome evolutions provide direct information about the magnitude of shocks that could also occur after treatment. This paper proposes a simple inference procedure that uses those pre-trends as the reference distribution for the post-treatment DID. The procedure is closely related to existing conformal inference procedures, but its DID-specific predictor leads to a distinct identifying restriction. Existing procedures assume parallel trends, while this paper's procedure does not require parallel trends.

title: The Architecture of Hybrid Warfare: Information, Cyber, and Influence Operations in Chinese and Russian Strategy

detail.title: The Architecture of Hybrid Warfare: Information, Cyber, and Influence Operations in Chinese and Russian Strategy
detail.abstract:
This working paper develops an integrated framework for understanding hybrid warfare as a multidomain system in which information, cyber, and cognitive operations converge to shape perceptions, emotions, and behaviors. While existing research often analyzes these components separately, this study synthesizes key academic and policy literature to demonstrate that influence operations-particularly cognitive and emotional manipulation-constitute the ultimate objective of hybrid warfare. 
Using this framework, the paper compares China and Russia across judicial, political, security, economic, informational, cyber, and cognitive domains. China employs long-term political warfare, legal instruments, economic leverage, and sustained cognitive operations against Taiwan and democratic societies. Russia integrates psychological operations with rapid kinetic action, using information and cyber tools to paralyze resistance prior to military intervention. 
The study offers a unified analytical model of contemporary authoritarian strategies and provides policy-relevant insights for strengthening democratic resilience, cognitive security, and multidomain defense.

title: Does Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Engagement Constrain Corporate Tax Avoidance? Evidence From Developing Economies: A Narrative Review
affiliations: and University of Delaware

detail.title: Does Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Engagement Constrain Corporate Tax Avoidance? Evidence From Developing Economies: A Narrative Review
detail.abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) engagement is often framed as a market-based constraint on aggressive corporate tax behavior, but developing-economy evidence is geographically concentrated, proxy-sensitive, and mostly associational. The review draws on 18 peer-reviewed, firm-level studies published from 2015 to early 2026, each involving firms from at least one World Bank low-or middle-income economy. Governance-related variables, especially board independence, audit oversight, and institutional ownership, were the most frequently reported ESG-related factors associated with lower tax avoidance. However, only a small minority of studies used quasi-experimental, instrumentalvariable, or dynamic-panel approaches capable of addressing endogeneity. Environmental-pillar evidence was sparse, and corporate social responsibility expenditure could not be treated as equivalent to standardized social-pillar ESG scores. Composite ESG findings were inconsistent, especially among Chinese A-share studies using similar rating sources. Current evidence supports cautious, targeted governance-focused pilots paired with stronger enforcement infrastructure, not broad reliance on composite ESG scores as tax-compliance tools.

title: Is it Always Rational for a Government to Monopolize Force? An Immanent Critique of the Statebuilding Literature
affiliations: Hamad Bin Khalifa University - College of Humanities and Social Sciences and Unaffilated Researcher

detail.title: Is it Always Rational for a Government to Monopolize Force? An Immanent Critique of the Statebuilding Literature
detail.abstract: We argue that it is not always rational for a government to monopolize force within its territorial domain. In particular, we consider governments under military occupation by a superior foreign power. Such a government is called upon by the occupier to consolidate a monopoly on force, wresting the means of violence from non-state militant groups that threaten the occupier with resistance. By complying with the occupier the indigenous government proves its loyalty to the occupier, but erodes its popular legitimacy. To manage this loyalty-legitimacy dilemma, governments may rationally choose to forgo a monopoly on force, coexisting with independent militant groups to whom they can outsource resistance. Thus, consolidating a territorial monopoly on the use of force is not the sine qua non of statebuilding that many political scientists believe it to be. Instead, in an important category of cases overrepresented in the statebuilding literature, force monopolization is sometimes irrational.

title: Symbiosis versus Crowding-Out under Moral Hazard: A Hidden-Action Counterpart to Jain (1999)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Symbiosis versus Crowding-Out under Moral Hazard: A Hidden-Action Counterpart to Jain (1999)
detail.abstract: It is common to find a bank and a moneylender lending to the same borrower, even though the bank's money is cheaper. This paper offers one reason. The bank cannot see whether its loan goes into the project or into the borrower's pocket. The informal lender charges more, but sits close enough to the borrower to keep an eye on what happens to its own money. A bank therefore uses this aspect of informal lender attribute by financing only a part of the project on purpose and letting the borrower to raise the rest locally. Thus, the borrower will have less bank money to be taken away. But in this lending structure cheap capital is being replaced by costly capital, which aspect of these two effects dominates decides the outcome. There are four outcomes are possible: full bank finance, full bank finance with a rent left to the borrower, joint formal-informal finance, and no lending at all. Co-financing is advisable when the private gain from diverting one more unit of capital of bank exceeds the informal lender's cost disadvantage. I then add a liquidity shock which raises the borrower's immediate need for cash. Diversion can then occur even when all borrowers look alike at the time of contracting. The policy results are not the same as in the adverse-selection argument of Jain (1999). A ceiling on formal repayment can bring down the informal share, and a rise in the cost of informal lending can lower welfare and, inside the joint-finance regime, make the bank ask for a larger informal contribution.

title: TOON-Based MultiFinRAG with Reinforcement Learning for Automated Stock Trading
affiliations: and Asia Pacific University of Technology and Innovation, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia

detail.title: TOON-Based MultiFinRAG with Reinforcement Learning for Automated Stock Trading
detail.abstract: Financial document analysis presents a persistent challenge for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems: the token-heavy nature of JSON-encoded financial tables rapidly exhausts language model context budgets, truncating the structured evidence required for numerical reasoning. This paper introduces the TOON-Based MultiFinRAG System, a unified five-module pipeline that couples Token-Oriented Object Notation (TOON) encoding with multimodal financial document retrieval, local large language model (LLM) inference, and deep reinforcement learning (RL) for automated equity trading. A controlled empirical study across 90 Apple Inc. (AAPL) 10-K financial tables demonstrates that TOON achieves a mean token reduction of 47.65% (median 48.81%, σ = 9.44%) relative to JSON, effectively doubling evidence capacity within fixed context windows. An event-driven, forward-filled LLM signal architecture based on SEC EDGAR filing dates eliminates look-ahead bias while preserving the temporal structure of fundamental information disclosure. A confidence-gated veto mechanism hierarchically integrates fundamental LLM signals with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) RL agent, blocking counter-regime trades when filing evidence is strong. Over a 250-day AAPL backtest (January 2025 to January 2026), PPO achieves the highest Sharpe ratio among five evaluated algorithms, consistent with its theoretical advantage in non-stationary financial environments. These findings establish TOON-based encoding as a practical pipeline enabler for compact, locally hosted language models operating under constrained context budgets, and demonstrate the feasibility of integrating fundamental filing signals with tactical reinforcement learning agents in a fully auditable, open-source framework.

title: From Signal Library to Portfolio: Redundancy, Marginal Information and Capital Allocation Across Systematic Signals

detail.title: From Signal Library to Portfolio: Redundancy, Marginal Information and Capital Allocation Across Systematic Signals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the principal of Guerrieri Capital Ltd, the private research vehicle through which this paper is published. The paper is methodological and research-oriented. It does not describe an investable product, recommend securities, disclose live positions, or present investor returns. The author received no external compensation or third-party funding for this work and declares no other personal or financial relationships that influenced the paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper does not involve patients, human participants, personal data, case studies, clinical material, animal subjects or experimental intervention.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received. The research was prepared independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper asks how a portfolio manager should distinguish a large signal catalogue from independent information, and whether an individually credible characteristic deserves capital. The central distinction is between evidence for a signal in isolation and its marginal contribution to the portfolio that would use it.
Evidence comes from two sources. A local reconstruction of the Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing catalogue contains 164 characteristics, 3,000 equities and 31.9 million observations between June 2016 and June 2026; a fixed coverage rule retains 112 characteristics. The public Open Asset Pricing archive supplies 112 US long-short predictor returns from January 1990 to December 2024. The local panel permits security-level tests of scores, overlap, marginal information and trading, while the public archive provides a longer comparison of historical predictor portfolio series.
The 112 local characteristics have a participation ratio effective rank of 37.05; alternative matrix constructions place it between 36.34 and 38.10. Six exact score-history relationships leave 106 representatives. Active coverage ranges from 80 to 112, and a constant set of 67 remains positive but weaker. Standalone evidence is incomplete: 75 characteristics have positive mean 21-session rank information in sterling, while 19 representatives are positive alone and negative against the full composite.
Return evidence depends materially on the population. The local equal signal composite is positive in the fixed panel in sterling, while the domestic US reconstruction does not confirm the result. The 112 public predictor portfolios are positive jointly over 1990-2024, but the evidence is weaker in the more recent period.
No allocation rule dominates consistently across populations, objectives and costs. The evidence therefore supports a decision standard rather than a universal weighting formula: capital should depend on credibility, distinct contribution, portfolio effect and implementation burden, each assessed against the portfolio that would own the signal.

title: Remittance-Led Resilience: A Structural Analysis of Bangladesh's Migrant Labour Economy, External Sector Stability, and the Post-LDC Graduation Transition

detail.title: Remittance-Led Resilience: A Structural Analysis of Bangladesh's Migrant Labour Economy, External Sector Stability, and the Post-LDC Graduation Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This independent research was conducted without any commercial or financial backing that could be construed as a conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a structural economic and macroeconomic analysis based entirely on publicly available secondary data from official institutions such as Bangladesh Bank, the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB), the IMF, the ADB, and the World Bank. As no human participants, patients, or primary field surveys were involved in this research, formal institutional ethics approval was not required
declarations.funderStatement: This study was conducted as an independent research study without external financial backing or institutional funding

detail.abstract: Two things have been holding up Bangladesh's external accounts for the last four fiscal years: money sent home by migrant workers, and garment exports. That's really the whole story in one sentence, and this paper spends the rest of its length unpacking it. Remittances hit a record US$35.56 billion in FY2025-26, roughly 17.3% more than the year before, and that money has done a lot of quiet work-steadying the taka, rebuilding reserves, giving households something to fall back on while the economy was still shaking off the mid-2024 political transition. I pulled together publicly available figures from Bangladesh Bank, the EPB, BGMEA, the IMF, the ADB, the World Bank, and CPD to trace where the remittances are actually coming from, what happened to RMG export earnings this year, and what risks are sitting ahead of the country as it heads toward LDC graduation on 24 November 2026. What the numbers show isn't quite the "everything's fine" story you tend to hear. Total merchandise exports actually fell 0.58% to US$48.00 billion in FY2025-26, and RMG exports on their own dropped 1.64% to US$38.70 billion-even as remittances grew by double digits for the second year running. So it's not that Bangladesh's external sector broadly held up; it's that one part of it did the heavy lifting while the other slipped. Add sub-trend GDP growth, inflation that hasn't really come down, private investment at a five-year low, and the coming erosion of preferential trade access, and the picture looks less like a resolved crisis and more like resilience that's being propped up from one side only. The paper ends with some thoughts on diversifying exports, formalising remittance channels, and getting through the graduation transition in one piece.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Market Development: The Roles of Energy Use and Foreign Direct Investment in Achieving a Green Economy and Carbon Neutrality in the United States
affiliations: Zhejiang University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Financial Market Development: The Roles of Energy Use and Foreign Direct Investment in Achieving a Green Economy and Carbon Neutrality in the United States
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial markets has fundamentally reshaped capital allocation, risk assessment, and investment strategies across the United States. Yet this transformation arrives at a critical juncture: the nation confronts an urgent imperative to decarbonize its economy and achieve carbon neutrality by mid-century. This article examines the tripartite relationship between AI-driven financial market development, energy consumption patterns, and foreign direct investment (FDI) flows, arguing that these forces collectively determine the trajectory of the United States toward a green economy. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, international energy projections, and financial market data, the analysis reveals that while AI enhances market efficiency and facilitates green capital mobilization, its substantial energy demands-particularly from data center infrastructurecreate a paradox that threatens to undermine climate objectives. Foreign direct investment emerges as a crucial mediating variable, channeling both capital and clean technology into domestic markets while also introducing competitive pressures that accelerate sustainable innovation. The article proposes a framework in which policy interventions must simultaneously address AI's energy footprint, incentivize green FDI, and reform financial market architectures to internalize carbon costs. The findings suggest that without coordinated governance, the United States risks a scenario in which AI-enabled financial growth exacerbates rather than alleviates environmental degradation, thereby compromising long-term carbon neutrality commitments.

title: Viability Leadership in Complex Systems

detail.title: Viability Leadership in Complex Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the originator of the Performance-Potential Crosshair and Viability Leadership frameworks discussed in this paper and is professionally active in strategy, leadership, and legal advisory services. He declares that he has no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived as having influenced, the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual and integrative review did not involve human participants, patients, animals, personal data, or primary empirical data collection. Therefore, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This conceptual working paper reassesses and advances the leadership framework introduced in Christoph Schließmann's 2014 book Leistungspotenziale im Fadenkreuz. The original model rejects universal leadership recipes and understands performance as a dynamic relationship among person, task, organization, relevant system, and time. It also conceptualizes organizational viability as a heuristic relation of agility and robustness to system complexity. An evidence-weighted integrative review of leadership research from January 2014 through 24 July 2026 examines leadership theory, organizational adaptability, psychological safety and employee voice, shared leadership, temporal person-environment fit, intuition, resilience, meaningful work and well-being, hybrid work, generative artificial intelligence, algorithmic management, and AI governance. Meta-analyses, systematic and integrative reviews, randomized field experiments, peerreviewed primary studies, and authoritative legal and governance sources are prioritized and triangulated. The review largely confirms the relational, systemic, and temporal premises of the 2014 model, while qualifying three claims: the viability equation is a theory heuristic rather than a calibrated metric; intuition is reliable only under identifiable conditions of expertise and feedback; and shared leadership requires vertical framing and accountability. Artificial intelligence adds a new governance dimension because leadership increasingly concerns coupled human-AI systems. The paper develops Viability Leadership as the dynamic meta-capability to preserve purposeful action, learning, and regeneration by continuously rebalancing agility, robustness, resonance, dynamic fit, and governance relative to complexity. Eight propositions and an empirical research agenda are presented.

title: From Registration to Repayment: Using Bidirectional Debt-Management Behavior as an Early Creditworthiness Signal for Data-Scarce Micro-Merchants in Saudi Arabia

detail.title: From Registration to Repayment: Using Bidirectional Debt-Management Behavior as an Early Creditworthiness Signal for Data-Scarce Micro-Merchants in Saudi Arabia
detail.abstract: Access to formal credit remains a persistent barrier for micro-merchants who lack the transaction history, digital footprint, or credit bureau records that alternative-data lending models typically rely on. While prior research has shown that digital transaction data, behavioral data, social network graphs, and psychometric assessments can improve credit risk assessment for underserved borrowers, these approaches share a common limitation: they all depend on applicants who already possess some minimal financial or digital footprint. Even psychometric tools, designed explicitly to bypass financial history, show weaker predictive power for applicants with no prior banking relationship at all. This gap is especially relevant in Saudi Arabia, where formal credit infrastructure for very small, informal retail businesses remains limited. This paper proposes a novel proxy signal for this underserved "no-file" segment: the bidirectional debt-management behavior micro-merchants exhibit from the moment they register on a digital ledger platform-specifically, how they manage receivables owed to them by customers alongside payables owed to their own suppliers. Unlike prior studies that model the creditworthiness of the end borrower, this framework inverts the analytical lens to examine whether a merchant's own financial management discipline can predict their own creditworthiness before any external lending relationship exists. Grounded in the Dayni platform-an early-stage debt-management application for Saudi micro-merchants-this paper presents a conceptual framework, a proposed variable set, and a staged empirical validation plan, positioning the approach for future testing as platform data matures.

title: The Political Economy of Mandatory Shareholder Arbitration
affiliations: Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and

detail.title: The Political Economy of Mandatory Shareholder Arbitration
detail.abstract:
For decades, mandatory arbitration provisions in corporate charters and bylaws—particularly those covering shareholder and federal securities claims—were widely regarded as both legally uncertain and practically unavailable. Their absence did not result from a single express prohibition, but from the interaction of federal regulatory practice and state corporate law. At the federal level, the Securities and Exchange Commission exercised informal but highly effective gatekeeping by opposing arbitration provisions in the IPO process. At the state level, Delaware law preserved judicial adjudication for internal corporate and securities claims, reinforcing a litigation-centered system of shareholder dispute resolution.

In 2025, the SEC disrupted this equilibrium by announcing that the presence of arbitration provisions would no longer affect the effectiveness of a registration statement. This policy shift removed the principal federal constraint and reopened the question whether arbitration may emerge as a viable governance mechanism for public companies. Yet the removal of legal barriers does not by itself determine governance outcomes.

This Article argues that the future of mandatory shareholder arbitration cannot be understood through legal doctrine alone. It must instead be analyzed through the political economy of corporate governance. The adoption of arbitration provisions will depend on the interaction of institutional incentives among Delaware, competing states, federal regulators, corporate managers, institutional investors, and the plaintiffs’ bar. Each of these actors has distinct—and often conflicting—interests in the structure of shareholder dispute resolution.

We show that Delaware’s resistance reflects the centrality of courts to its governance model and the importance of precedent production to its dominance in the market for corporate charters. The SEC’s shift toward disclosure-based regulation, by contrast, reallocates decision-making authority from the regulator to market actors. Institutional investors, managers, and litigation intermediaries further shape the landscape through their responses to arbitration’s potential effects on enforcement, accountability, and litigation risk.

The Article concludes that the persistence of shareholder litigation reflects not merely legal constraints, but a broader institutional equilibrium. The evolution of shareholder arbitration, much like the evolution of corporate governance more generally, depends not only on changes in legal doctrine, but also on the interaction of institutional forces that determine which governance mechanisms are viable—and sustainable—in practice.

 Mandatory arbitration provisions may now be legally conceivable in ways that they were not before, but their widespread adoption remains uncertain. It may ultimately depend on whether early adopters can shift market expectations and perceptions associated with such provisions, much as early adopters of dual-class stock—such as Google and Facebook—contributed to its widespread use, especially among technology companies.

title: Beyond Average Accuracy: Statistical Distinguishability and Temporal Concentration in Data-Rich Macroeconomic Forecasting

detail.title: Beyond Average Accuracy: Statistical Distinguishability and Temporal Concentration in Data-Rich Macroeconomic Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available aggregate macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or clinical interventions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Machine-learning forecasts can achieve lower average errors than simple benchmarks without establishing a statistically distinguishable or persistent advantage. This study examines those distinctions in a fixed-length rolling pseudo-out-of-sample exercise using the dated June 2026 FRED-MD vintage, frozen in July 2026. Four U.S. monthly targets—CPI inflation, PCE inflation, industrial production growth, and the monthly change in unemployment—are forecast at horizons of 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. The comparison covers nine individual models and three forecast combinations, using 360-month estimation windows and up to 90 target months from December 2018 through May 2026. XGBoost records the lowest average relative RMSE (0.821) against transformed-series persistence, followed closely by the random-forest variants; the forecast combinations also deliver sizable numerical gains. Formal inference is much less conclusive. After Holm adjustment, none of the 176 squared-error Diebold-Mariano comparisons rejects equal predictive accuracy in favor of an alternative. Five absolute-error comparisons do so, all at the one-month industrial-production horizon. A 90% Model Confidence Set retains all twelve approaches in 25 of 32 target-horizon-loss panels and never retains fewer than ten. Rankings also vary over time: in 12-month rolling evaluations, the winner set changes between adjacent windows in 18% to 38% of cases. Within each model-target-horizon cell, the twelve largest favorable and unfavorable monthly contributions account, on average, for 85.6% of gross improvements and 89.1% of gross deteriorations relative to the benchmark. These patterns persist under longer ranking windows, and the average gain falls sharply when the benchmark's largest-error dates are removed. Lower average loss, statistical distinguishability, and temporal durability are therefore separate properties. For this short, shock-heavy sample, the evidence favors reporting forecast combinations and uncertainty diagnostics alongside the leading models rather than treating a single ex post winner as definitive.

title: A Theory of Country-Sensitive Financial Modelling (CSFMT): A Conceptual Foundation for Institutional Adaptation in Comparative Financial Systems
affiliations: Institute of Certified Public Accountant ( ICPAP)

detail.title: A Theory of Country-Sensitive Financial Modelling (CSFMT): A Conceptual Foundation for Institutional Adaptation in Comparative Financial Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or other conflicts of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a conceptual theory-building paper based on literature synthesis, logical deduction, and cross-disciplinary integration. It does not involve human participants, human data, animals, clinical research, surveys, interviews, or experiments requiring ethics committee or institutional review board approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was independently conceived, developed, and completed by the author.

detail.abstract:
The increasing globalization of financial decision-making has encouraged the widespread application of quantitative financial models across jurisdictions with fundamentally different institutional, regulatory, legal, and governance environments. Although this practice has improved analytical consistency, it has also reinforced the implicit assumption that financial models are universally transferable, regardless of institutional context. Existing research has extensively examined institutional diversity, comparative financial systems, legal origins, and governance quality; however, it has not established a comprehensive theoretical foundation explaining how financial models should adapt when applied across institutionally diverse environments.

This paper addresses this gap by developing the Theory of Country-Sensitive Financial Modelling (CSFMT), which argues that financial models are conditionally rather than universally transferable. Using a conceptual theory-building approach based on knowledge synthesis, logical deduction, and cross-disciplinary integration, the study develops the core assumptions, foundational principles, theoretical propositions, and progressive adaptation levels that collectively explain institutional adaptation in financial modelling. The paper further introduces the Alaali Country Adaptation Layer (A-CAL) as the conceptual mechanism through which institutional adaptation can be systematically incorporated within the broader Alaali Financial Models Meta-Framework (AFMF), a conceptual architecture for adaptive financial modelling.

The study contributes to the literature by establishing CSFMT as a new theoretical perspective linking institutional distance to financial model applicability, introducing a progressive adaptation theory comprising Contextual, Parametric, and Structural Adaptation, and positioning institutional adaptation as a fundamental determinant of financial model design rather than merely a contextual consideration. The proposed framework offers conceptual guidance for financial analysts, regulators, policymakers, and researchers, particularly within the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and other emerging-market environments. Future research should focus on operationalizing the theory through empirical validation, adaptation indices, decision-support methodologies, and software assisted implementation. By positioning institutional compatibility as a fundamental determinant of financial model applicability, CSFMT establishes a new conceptual direction for comparative financial modelling that balances global analytical consistency with local institutional relevance.

title: Form Without Substance? Charter Capital and the Limits of Creditor Protection in Azerbaijani Corporate Law

detail.title: Form Without Substance? Charter Capital and the Limits of Creditor Protection in Azerbaijani Corporate Law
detail.abstract: This paper examines charter capital as a legal institution under the Civil Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan (Articles 87-105-1), tracing its concept, functions, formation, and protective role across limited liability companies, joint-stock companies, partnerships, and entities with additional liability. Charter capital is generally presented as a straightforward guarantee: a minimum fund that secures creditors' interests from the moment of incorporation. This paper argues that the guarantee is more limited, and more dependent on institutional enforcement, than that presentation suggests. Comparative analysis of German, French, Russian, British, and American company law shows that capital thresholds-whether strict, as in Germany, or largely abandoned, as in the United Kingdom and the United States-protect creditors only where they are backed by credible valuation of non-monetary contributions, effective net-asset monitoring, and enforceable consequences for undercapitalization. Azerbaijani law contains each of these mechanisms in formal terms, through the net-asset rules of Articles 90.4 and 103.5, the mandatory-contribution rules of Articles 90.3 and 103.4, and the general framework governing capital increase and reduction, but their practical bite depends on enforcement capacity that the Civil Code itself does not supply. The U.S. case Kinney Shoe Corp. v. Polan is used as a comparative illustration of what happens when capital rules are formally present but substantively unobserved. The paper concludes that Azerbaijan's reform priority should not be abandoning the civil-law capital model, but closing the gap between its formal architecture and its practical enforcement.

title: From Static Knowledge Assets to Verifiable agent Assets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Static Knowledge Assets to Verifiable agent Assets

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual and protocol-design study did not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects, experiments, surveys, interviews, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
As artificial agents move from passive software tools toward persistent, networked systems that discover
one another, invoke external services, delegate tasks, and generate measurable economic value, the
conventional objects of digital ownership become increasingly inadequate. Prompts, code repositories, model
weights, and workflow files may remain valuable, but they are readily copied, regenerated, forked, or
separated from their creators and from the execution histories that make them commercially credible. This
paper proposes the concept of a Verifiable Agent Asset (VAA): a persistent, economically addressable agent
object that binds identity, controller and creator relationships, capability provenance, version lineage,
authorization and licensing terms, signed execution receipts, contextual reputation, economic-right
mappings, and lifecycle controls. The contribution is not a new cryptographic identity primitive. Rather, it is
an institutional-technical synthesis that connects existing building blocks - including Agent2Agent discovery,
decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, software supply-chain attestations, authenticated delegation,
and reputation evidence - into an asset envelope suitable for licensing, attribution, audit, revenue allocation,
and revocation. The framework is explicitly distinct from legal personhood: an agent is treated as a verifiable
carrier of rights and obligations assigned to human or organizational principals, not as an autonomous owner
by default. The paper also connects this architecture to temporal sovereignty. If agents are permitted to earn
but their indefinite autonomous accumulation must remain bounded, economic value first needs a traceable
carrier through which permissions, revenue claims, operational capital, and accumulation constraints can be
enforced. The proposed framework supplies that carrier and establishes the middle layer between a normative
theory of AI wealth boundaries and a future agent economic protocol governing multi-agent transactions.
