No personally identifiable information, such as names or contact details, was collected, and all responses were analysed in aggregate to maintain participant confidentiality. Completion of the questionnaire was considered as implied consent to participate in the study.

detail.abstract: The fast growth of food delivery applications and social media has changed the way consumers discover restaurants, select food options, and make purchasing decisions. This study aimed to examine the combined influence of food delivery applications and social media on the consumer decision-making and food purchasing behaviour of Generation Z consumers in Mumbai. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted, and primary data were collected through an online questionnaire administered to 204 respondents using convenience and snowball sampling. The findings indicate that factors such as convenience, discounts, delivery speed, visually appealing content, and social media engagement significantly influence consumer purchasing behaviour. The study also found that Generation Z increasingly relies on digital platforms when making food-related decisions. The findings support the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), suggesting that technological and social factors together shape consumer behaviour. The study contributes to the growing literature on digital consumer behaviour by examining the combined influence of food delivery applications and social media within the context of Generation Z consumers in Mumbai.

title: Christian Royal Priesthood Identity and Its Influence on Luxury Fashion Consumption

detail.title: Christian Royal Priesthood Identity and Its Influence on Luxury Fashion Consumption
detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of Christian royal priesthood identity on luxury fashion consumption through an interdisciplinary analysis of theology, consumer psychology, fashion studies, and cultural identity. Drawing from the biblical concept of believers as a “royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9, KJV), this research explores how sacred identity shapes perceptions of beauty, adornment, self-presentation, and material expression. Through a qualitative theological-interpretive methodology, the study analyzes biblical texts concerning priesthood, kingship, holiness, and symbolic garments alongside contemporary scholarship on religious consumer behavior, luxury consumption, and fashion identity. The findings suggest that Christian royal priesthood identity does not inherently reject luxury fashion but transforms its meaning by reframing luxury as a potential expression of dignity, stewardship, spiritual representation, and consecrated identity. Rather than viewing luxury solely through the lenses of status signaling or materialism, this framework positions fashion as a symbolic medium through which believers negotiate faith, culture, and personal identity. The study further identifies three primary influences of royal priesthood identity on luxury consumption: symbolic self-presentation, spiritually motivated consumption, and ethical boundaries shaped by holiness and stewardship. By integrating biblical theology with consumer psychology and fashion theory, this research contributes to emerging discussions on religion’s role in marketplace behavior and challenges assumptions that luxury fashion is inherently secular. The study proposes that Christian identity functions as a significant interpretive framework through which luxury goods acquire theological, cultural, and symbolic meaning.

title: The Marketing Context Graph: A Governed Substrate for Causal Marketing Measurement and Auditable Decision Provenance Causal Inference as a Governed Layer on a Bitemporal Context Graph
affiliations: Lifesight and Lifesight

detail.title: The Marketing Context Graph: A Governed Substrate for Causal Marketing Measurement and Auditable Decision Provenance Causal Inference as a Governed Layer on a Bitemporal Context Graph

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Both authors are employees of Lifesight, a company that develops AI augmented unified marketing measurement SaaS including media-mix modelling and incrementality tooling; Anil Kumar Singh is its CTO and co-founder. The Marketing Context Graph described in this paper reflects an architecture in commercial development at Lifesight, a relationship that could be perceived as an interest in its favourable evaluation. The contribution is methodological: all reported results derive from synthetic data with known ground truth and openly released code; no proprietary dataset, customer data, or commercial product is evaluated or benchmarked, and all comparisons are against standard public methods. The authors declare no other competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research involves no human participants, patients, animal subjects, or personal data; all results derive from computer simulations on synthetic data with known ground truth.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted by the authors as employees of Lifesight, which provided no funding beyond their regular employment.

detail.abstract:
Marketing decisions increasingly depend on two capabilities that have evolved separately: causal marketing measurement (distinguishing real advertising effects from the correlational patterns in marketing data, the domain of Causal AI) and governed, graph-based context for the AI agents now trusted to act on those effects, the domain of Agentic AI. Both are limited by the same architectural gap. 
Problem 1: measurement is correlational by construction (not only in media-mix models but in touch-based attribution and observational methods generally), so a channel’s direct, indirect, and total effects are hard to separate and to calibrate against experiments. Problem 2: the agents acting on those effects lack persistent, governed, historically accurate context, and to answer questions such as which campaigns to scale or how to optimize the mix they must reason over incremental effects, uncertainty, evidence strength, applicable populations, and decision lineage, not language.

We introduce the Marketing Context Graph (MCG), a bi-temporal, governed property graph, formally a tuple G = (E, R, γE, γR), in which campaign entities, spend vectors, conversion outcomes, and external macro factors are connected by typed, directional, causally identified edges carrying bi-temporal attributes and reified decision traces. We give it a precise set-theoretic semantics, define a point-in-time snapshot operator Σ(tv, tr), and prove it is free of look-ahead contamination. Crucially, the MCG is a governed substrate, not a new estimator: the measurement methods applied on it are classical: mediation / path analysis, inverse-probability weighting, and transport. We (i) inject an experiment-identified halo edge as an informative structural prior into a Gaussian-conjugate Bayesian MMM, showing it reduces posterior variance along the collinear directions (Remark 1) while separating that variance claim from identification (Proposition 2); (ii) compose each channel’s total effect by traversing the graph, so budget decisions improve as cross-channel mediation grows and gain nothing when no structure exists; (iii) reconstruct complete, auditable decision provenance; and (iv) transport an identified edge across populations exactly when the graph’s selection diagram licenses it, and refuse when it does not.

Our evaluation is decision-centric rather than fit-centric. Across 8,000 simulated budget decisions the graph cuts budget-decision regret by up to 43% as cross-channel mediation grows (a paired within-replication reduction); look-ahead-free backtesting exposes 70% over-investment that a flat store conceals; the graph answers the provenance queries that require multi-hop, policy, temporal, and audit structure a flat fact/vector store cannot represent; and governed transport stays low-error as populations diverge, where naive transfer’s error grows linearly with divergence. Evidence is synthetic by design, isolating each mechanism against a known oracle; all results are reproducible from released code.

title: Personal Intellectual Capital: A Framework for Professional Excellence in the AI Era

detail.title: Personal Intellectual Capital: A Framework for Professional Excellence in the AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual contribution and does not involve human participants, data collection, or experimental procedures; accordingly, no ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes Personal Intellectual Capital (Personal IC) as a micro-foundational framework explaining how knowledge workers configure, govern and mobilise intellectual resources to sustain Professional Excellence in AI-mediated knowledge work. It addresses a persistent theoretical gap: while Intellectual Capital and Knowledge Management research explain how organisations create value from intangible resources, they provide limited explanation of how individuals do so. Personal IC is conceptualised as an evolving configuration of Human, Structural and Relational intellectual resources whose value is realised through Human Agency (governance) and Knowledge-inAction (enactment). Following a formal theory-building methodology, the paper synthesises Intellectual Capital, Knowledge Management, and Artificial Intelligence research into a causal framework with five theoretical propositions. The framework specifies a causal architecture in which Personal Intellectual Capital provides intellectual potential, Human Agency governs and orchestrates its mobilisation, Knowledge-inAction represents its enactment, and Professional Excellence emerges through sustained value-creating professional contribution. This is captured by the Direction Imperative: as AI-generated knowledge becomes abundant, purposeful human direction becomes the primary source of differentiation in knowledge work. The paper advances Intellectual Capital theory by providing a causal framework for Individual-Level Intellectual Capital, contributing the tripartite architecture of Personal IC, positioning Human Agency as the governance mechanism linking intellectual resources to action, introducing Knowledge-inAction as the enactment mechanism, conceptualising Professional Excellence as sustained value creation in AI-mediated knowledge work, and proposing the Direction Imperative to explain why AImediated knowledge abundance increases-rather than diminishes-the strategic importance of human intellectual capital.

title: The Covenantal Marketing Framework: Proposing a Biblically Inspired Model for Silent Marketing in Luxury and Fashion Through the Lens of Semiotics, Iconography and Psychology

detail.title: The Covenantal Marketing Framework: Proposing a Biblically Inspired Model for Silent Marketing in Luxury and Fashion Through the Lens of Semiotics, Iconography and Psychology
detail.abstract: This study introduces the Covenantal Marketing Framework, a biblically inspired conceptual model that reinterprets luxury and fashion marketing through the integrated lenses of semiotics, iconography, psychology, and theological aesthetics. Challenging dominant marketing paradigms centered on persuasion, dominance, and status signaling, this research proposes “silent marketing” as an alternative framework rooted in symbolic restraint, spiritual intentionality, and covenantal meaning. Through qualitative conceptual analysis of existing literature on luxury consumption, consumer psychology, religious orientation, branding, and visual communication, the study examines how products, environments, and brand rituals function as semiotic systems that communicate identity, values, and transcendence. Drawing from Christian theology and biblical principles, the framework argues that luxury can operate not as a mechanism of social elevation or material performance, but as a vessel of stewardship, testimony, and sacred expression. The study further explores how Christian consumers interpret luxury symbolism through moral cognition, spiritual identity, and theological discernment, demonstrating that marketplace behavior is shaped not only by psychological motivations but also by faith-based meaning systems. By reframing branding as revelation, design as testimony, and consumer engagement as covenantal participation, this research contributes a spiritually grounded perspective to luxury marketing scholarship. The Covenantal Marketing Framework expands discussions of branding beyond transactional exchange, proposing that luxury communication can function as a symbolic language of purpose, legacy, and divine alignment.

title: Moving Targets: Promissory Instability in the Pricing and Access Terms of Generative AI Subscription Services (2024-2026)

detail.title: Moving Targets: Promissory Instability in the Pricing and Access Terms of Generative AI Subscription Services (2024-2026)
detail.abstract: Between October 2024 and July 2026, the leading commercial providers of generative artificial intelligence repeatedly modified the pricing, usage limits, and access terms of subscription services after consumers had already paid for them. This paper documents that pattern through a rapid multiple-case documentary analysis of four providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Moonshot AI), drawing exclusively on dated public sources: official announcements, technology press coverage, community bug trackers, and the public record of two formal legal actions. Seventeen documented episodes are organized into a chronology and classified with a two-dimensional framework defined by the trigger of the change (exogenous shocks of capacity, regulation, or safety versus endogenous commercial strategy) and the quality of its communication (managed transitions versus unmanaged or repeatedly revised promises). Two findings emerge. First, post-purchase modification is not an incident but an industry-wide operating pattern, and it moves in both directions: restrictions and reversals, price increases and price cuts. Second, formal accountability (a proposed class action against Anthropic over advertised Claude Max usage multipliers and a regulatory enforcement action against Microsoft over Copilot-linked price increases) concentrates in one quadrant of the framework: endogenous changes communicated in unmanaged or shifting ways. The paper argues that this instability is a structural consequence of selling elastic promises against inelastic compute, discusses implications for consumer protection in AI markets, and proposes an agenda for longitudinal, archive-based tracking of subscription terms.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work: Forecasting Occupational Polarization Using Attention -LSTM

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work: Forecasting Occupational Polarization Using Attention -LSTM
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming labor markets by reshaping occupational structures, skill requirements, and workforce dynamics. Despite growing evidence on AI exposure and automation risks, limited research has examined how occupa tional polarization may evolve under accelerating AI diffusion. This study investigates the future evolution of labor market polarization using an Attention-LSTM forecasting framework that integrates macroeconomic indicators, AI adoption proxies, occupatio nal characteristics derived from O*NET, and AI-related sentiment measures extracted through FinBERT. Using an occupation-level dataset covering 873 occupations, the model generates scenario-based forecasts of occupational trajectories through 2030 , and evaluates their distribution across alternative development scenarios. The results reveal a substantial restructuring of the occupational landscape. Safe Zone occupations decline from 517 occupations in 2021 to zero by 2028, while Dead Zone occupations expand to 636 occupations by 2030. A structural tipping point emerges between 2026 and 2027, characterized by a rapid increase in automation-vulnerable occupations and a simultaneous expansion of AI-complementary occupations. The findings highlight the un even nature of AI-driven labor market transformation and underscore the importance of workforce adaptation, reskilling policies, and technology governance in increasingly AI-intensive economies.

title: The Promotion Lift Trap: Targeting, Operational Filtering, and Weak Counterfactuals in Promotion Measurement

detail.title: The Promotion Lift Trap: Targeting, Operational Filtering, and Weak Counterfactuals in Promotion Measurement
detail.abstract: Promotion reports often call the response difference between promoted and comparison groups "lift." The label is causal only when the comparison group represents what promoted customers would have done without the promotion. This note examines one way that credibility can fail. Commercial targeting selects customers who appear valuable, responsive, reachable, eligible, or otherwise actionable. Delivery then applies further operational filters. If the comparison group does not reconstruct both processes, measured lift combines the promotion's effect with a pre-treatment baseline gap. A simulation of 100,000 synthetic customers isolates this mechanism. It assigns every customer the same two-percentage-point treatment effect and compares expected response probabilities rather than sampled outcomes. A valid holdout reports 1.9 percentage points of lift. Commercial targeting against the unselected residual reports 10.1 points; asymmetric reachability filtering reports 4.2 points. Matching reduces the error only when its variables and candidate pool approximate the targeting and delivery process. The broad ordering is stable on average, although a few sensitivity cells reverse. The exercise demonstrates a possible failure mode, not its prevalence in any industry. The managerial implication is narrow but important. Response is not incrementality. A representative-looking control can still be wrong if it reflects the population rather than the process that produced the treated group.

title: Australia's Occupational Transformation, 2006-2021

detail.title: Australia's Occupational Transformation, 2006-2021

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no declaration of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: The paper relies upon Census data that is public
declarations.funderStatement: The research was not funded

detail.abstract: This paper examines the extent to which changes in the Australian occupational structure between 2006 and 2021 reflected proportional demographic growth. Using occupational data derived from the Australian Census, growth rates for 476 occupational categories are compared against benchmarks for population and total employment growth. The analysis demonstrates that occupational change was highly uneven. While Australia's population increased by approximately 28 per cent and total employment by approximately 32 per cent during the period, many occupations substantially exceeded these benchmarks whereas others experienced little growth or absolute decline. Health and aged care occupations, information and communications technology, policy and planning, and professional advisory services expanded at rates that were several multiples of demographic growth. Conversely, clerical support, manufacturing-related occupations and numerous agricultural occupations contracted despite continued population expansion. Labour market adjustment was not incremental but highly polarised. The size of an occupation in 2006 had little relationship with its subsequent rate of growth, implying that structural forces rather than historical occupational composition determined labour demand. The findings support the proposition that Australia experienced a transformation of its workforce rather than a simple proportional expansion of employment. Technological change, demographic ageing, institutional developments and the increasing importance of knowledge-intensive services collectively reshaped the occupational landscape.

title: ROOT: A Framework for Closing the Data-Decision Gap in Complex Organizations

detail.title: ROOT: A Framework for Closing the Data-Decision Gap in Complex Organizations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted independently and does not represent any company intellectual property or official positions. No financial conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received. Independent research.

detail.abstract: Organizations consistently fail to convert data investments into decision quality improvements. This paper proposes ROOT-a sequenced framework addressing four structural deficiencies: the absence of explicit decision architecture (R), the confusion between org chart and operating model (O), the premature deployment of intelligence layers before governance exists (O), and the unresolved trust-territory tension that determines whether the first three can function (T). The evidentiary support is deliberately tiered and declared as such. The Real Decision System (R) rests on peer-reviewed decision science (Kahneman, Sibony & Sunstein, 2021; Vroom & Yetton, 1973; Howard, 1966). Outcome-Layered Intelligence (O2) rests on medium-confidence industry surveys with temporal caveats (MIT Sloan/BCG, 2019; O'Reilly, 2019). The Operating Model (O1) rests on IS canon and practitioner authority (Waterman et al., 1980; Wixom & Watson, 2001) and lacks controlled studies specific to analytics-team design-a limitation stated openly. The fourth component, Trust as enabling substrate, is grounded in multiple converging research streams-algorithm aversion (Dietvorst, Simmons & Massey, 2015), business-IT alignment (Luftman, Papp & Brier, 1999), BI adoption (Wixom & Watson, 2001), and large-firm practitioner surveys (Bean & Davenport, 2021)-and advanced as a directional hypothesis pending empirical validation in analytics-specific organizational contexts. The framework targets analytics leaders in complex, multi-country organizations operating under data scarcity-specifically LATAM pharma and FMCG contexts-where existing frameworks (RAPID, DACI, Gartner Analytics Maturity) address partial problems without integrating the full causal chain.

title: We Are What We Buy: Extracting Urban Lifestyles using Large-sScale Delivery Records
affiliations: Inha University, Korea University,  and KDI School of Public Policy and Management

detail.title: We Are What We Buy: Extracting Urban Lifestyles using Large-sScale Delivery Records

publicationDetails.detailsText: KDI School of Pub Policy & Management Paper No. DS26-04
publicationDetails.journalName: KDI School of Public Policy & Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Lifestyle has been used as a lens to characterize a society and its people within, which includes their social status, consumption habits, values, and cultural interests. Recently, the increasing availability of large-scale purchasing records, such as credit card transaction data, has enabled data-driven studies to capture lifestyles through consumption behavior. However, the lack of detailed information on individual purchases prevents researchers from constructing a precise representation of lifestyle structures through the consumption pattern. Here, we extract urban lifestyle patterns as a composition of fine-grained product categories that are significantly consumed together. Leveraging 103,342,186 package delivery records from 2018 to 2022 in Seoul, Republic of Korea, we construct a co-consumption network of detailed product categories and systematically identify lifestyles as clusters in the network. Our results reveal five lifestyle clusters-Beauty lovers, Fashion lovers, Work and life, Homemakers, and Baby and hobbyists-representing distinctive lifestyles, while also being connected to each other. Moreover, the geospatial distribution of lifestyle clusters aligns with regional characteristics (business vs. residential areas) and is associated with multiple demographic characteristics of residents, such as income, birth rate, and age. Temporal analysis further demonstrates that lifestyle patterns evolve in response to external disruptions, such as COVID-19. As urban societies become more multi-faceted, our framework provide a powerful tool for researchers, policymakers, and businesses to understand the shifting dynamics of contemporary lifestyles.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study investigates the mediating role of consumer engagement (CE) in the relationship between perceived behavioral control (PBC) and purchase intent and the moderating role of perceived safety in the relationship between PBC and CE in the self-driving car (SDC) context. Design/methodology/approach-To test the model, a sample of 368 consumers was deployed using partial least-squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings-The findings reveal that consumers' SDC engagement mediates the relationship between PBC and their intent to purchase an SDC. Consumer-perceived SDC safety also moderates the association of PBC/ engagement. Originality/value-While prior research has examined consumer-based drivers of SDC adoption, understanding of consumers' SDC engagement-related dynamics and outcomes lags behind. Addressing this gap, we propose and test a model that explores consumers' SDC engagement visa -vis its drivers (perceived SDC safety/behavioral control) and outcomes (SDC purchase intent).

detail.abstract: A pre-product-market-fit founder selling low-priced software cannot buy a measurement. Paid platforms withhold delivery optimization below roughly fifty optimization events per ad set per week, which prices the minimum viable measurement at $500 to $2,000 a week against the $15-50 such a founder can put behind an entire test; organic motions return their verdict in quarters, after the decision window has closed. The loop does not break; it starves. This paper prices that impossibility and scopes it honestly, since what the floor bounds is measurement rather than response, and then develops the exit: price the decision instead of the estimate, and move the measured event upstream, where base rates run an order of magnitude higher. The instrument is a break-even bar derived from the founder's own unit economics, a fixed budget of hand-targeted acts logged in a ten-token schema, and a pre-committed Wilson-bound stopping rule mapping onto Kill / Pivot / Double-Down. Its exact operating characteristics are computed and published here, including the defect that computing them found: as first frozen, the rule approved a batch on one reply to one touch, and the minimum-sample guard that repairs it is dated and disclosed rather than quietly merged. A second measurement bounds the protocol from the other side: of 114 real, recently launched products read through the instrument, 50 carry no pricing signal at all, so for 44% of that sample the break-even bar cannot be derived from public information and must be set deliberately or not at all. The paper's remaining empirical content is about its own instrument rather than its market. It reports nine dated errors this paper's own production pipeline caught before any reader was exposed, a coverage census over every externally checkable claim in it, and nine rows contributed to the predecessor paper's correction-latency-gap construct. Part II then reviews what deployed agentic marketing systems have actually shipped, states the two regularities they obey, and identifies an empty cell: no self-modifying agent has ever been tested against a reward that is simultaneously real, delayed, human-mediated, and adversarial. Zero field acts exist as of this draft, and the paper says so wherever it matters.

title: Building Customer Relationships While Achieving Sales Performance Results: Is Listening the Holy Grail of Sales ?
affiliations: , Illinois State University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Building Customer Relationships While Achieving Sales Performance Results: Is Listening the Holy Grail of Sales ?
detail.abstract: Despite its importance in sales, listening is an overlooked concept in research with limited empirical studies examining the construct since the work conducted by Castleberry and Shepherd (1993) and Ramsey and Sohi (1997). Knowledge of the role listening plays in sales and the processes involved in explaining listening in relationship performance is limited with many discrepancies identified between studies. Using meta-analytical techniques, this study summarizes approximately 20 years of research on salesperson listening. The study developed a meta-analytical model based on the marketing and psychology literature to build an underlying framework for listening theory, advance research in listening, and provide theoretical and managerial implications. The obtained results show that customer-oriented salespeople express their care toward customers through listening, which helps them adapt their selling behaviors to fit customers' demands. Salesperson relational and sales outcomes are driven by listening through direct and mediated mechanisms.

title: The Hidden Cost of Online Entry: Add-on Services and Brick-and-Mortar Market Density
affiliations: , Southern University of Science and Technology, Southern University of Science and Technology and

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Online Entry: Add-on Services and Brick-and-Mortar Market Density
detail.abstract: Brick-and-mortar (BM) firms face growing pressure from online competition but can respond strategically by leveraging physically anchored add-on services. We develop a Salop model with a location-free e-tailer to examine how online competition shapes BM firms' service provision, profitability, market density, and welfare outcomes. Add-on service emerges as a strategic response to online competition: BM firms deter online entry when service costs are low, coexist with the e-tailer at intermediate costs, and abandon service when costs are high. For a fixed BM market density, the presence of the e-tailer reduces BM profits but benefits consumers by disciplining product-service offerings and expanding online access. These benefits need not persist, however, once BM entry and exit are endogenous. By weakening BM profitability, online competition can contract the local BM network, concentrate demand among surviving firms, and increase aggregate transportation and service-congestion costs, thereby reducing consumer surplus below the BM-only benchmark. This hidden cost is most pronounced when the online channel is strong enough to erode local BM coverage but not strong enough to replace the nearby offline services that consumers lose. Our findings caution that regulators should evaluate online expansion not only through its competitive-discipline and access benefits, but also through its effect on local market structure and consumer surplus.

title: Semiotics of The Creator of The Universe
affiliations: Universitas Muhammadiyah Tangerang

detail.title: Semiotics of The Creator of The Universe
detail.abstract:
This book advances a single, deliberately unfashionable claim: the Qur'an is a book of signs, not a book of science. Against the widespread apologetic tradition of iʿjāz ʿilmī, which seeks to validate revelation by matching its verses to contemporary scientific findings, the study argues that this very project diminishes the text it means to defend. When revelation is treated as a repository of scientific propositions awaiting empirical confirmation, its standing is made hostage to theories that, by their own nature, are designed to be superseded. What is intended as a defence becomes a reduction.

Drawing on the semiotic frameworks of Saussure, Peirce, Barthes, and Eco, the book develops what it terms a semiotics of tawḥīd: an approach that retains the descriptive apparatus of the discipline while holding that the chain of signification does not terminate in endless cultural convention but converges upon the Creator. Within this framework, the cosmic verses (āyāt kawniyyah) and the scriptural verses (āyāt qurʾāniyyah) function alike as signs phenomena that do not rest in themselves but direct the attentive reader beyond them. The book grounds this reading in a close examination of the Qur'anic text, showing that mentions of natural phenomena are characteristically bound to an outward-directing closing formula whose removal would empty the verse of its function.

The argument advances a symmetrical critique of two opposed errors: scientism, which halts at empirical mechanism and denies that signs point beyond the measurable, and rigid literalism, which halts at the surface of the word and freezes meaning in the letter. Both, the study contends, fail for the same reason each treats what it encounters as terminating in itself. Between these, the book locates the reading that Iqra' bismi rabbik prescribes: attentive to the phenomenon, faithful to the text, yet following each sign in the direction it points.

Organised into nine parts and thirty-four chapters, the work traces the reading of signs across nature, the self, history, language, society, and the circumstances of a human life trial, sustenance, and death before extending it from the individual reader to education, science, daʿwah, and the vision of a civilisation of meaning. Written by a scholar of communication studies, it treats the question of revelation not merely as one of exegesis but as one of communication in its most fundamental sense: how a message is conveyed, how a sign is apprehended, and why the same sign yields differently to different readers. The book does not attempt to prove the existence of God, nor to fix a single correct interpretation of any verse. It offers, more modestly, a way of reading that accords revelation and science their respective places without requiring the sacrifice of either.

title: Because You Are a Part of Me”: Assessing the Effects of Salesperson Social Media Use on Job Outcomes and The Moderating Roles of Moral Identity and Gender
affiliations: , University of Dayton, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - E.J. Ourso College of Business Administration and Institute of Management Technology, Ghaziabad

detail.title: Because You Are a Part of Me”: Assessing the Effects of Salesperson Social Media Use on Job Outcomes and The Moderating Roles of Moral Identity and Gender
detail.abstract: Although the effects of salesperson social media use have recently received significant scholarly attention, there remains critical research gaps that, if addressed, can further broaden our understanding of the impact of salesperson social media use in business-to-business settings. Grounded in construal level theory and the related psychological distance framework, we suggest that salesperson social media use increases salesperson inclusion-ofthe-customer-in-the-self by reducing the psychological distance between the salesperson and their respective customers. More so, we posit that this relationship is positively moderated by salesperson moral identity, such that the relationship is strengthened at higher levels of moral identity. Furthermore, we identify a potential three-way interaction by considering the role of salesperson gender in driving this interactive relationship. Our results, based on survey responses from 158 business-to-business salespeople, lend support to our theoretical model and shows that the moderating effect of salesperson moral identity on the relationship between salesperson social media use and salesperson inclusion-of-customer-in-the-self is stronger for females than it is for males. Additionally, we find that salesperson inclusion-of-customer-in-the-self is related to higher salesperson customer knowledge, which, ultimately, improves salesperson performance. In the light of our findings, we discuss subsequent managerial and theoretical implications.

title: Us” To Co-Create Value and Hate” Them”: Examining the Interplay of” Consumer-Brand Identification, Peer Identification, Value Co-Creation Among Consumers, Competitor Brand Hate and Individualism

detail.title: Us” To Co-Create Value and Hate” Them”: Examining the Interplay of” Consumer-Brand Identification, Peer Identification, Value Co-Creation Among Consumers, Competitor Brand Hate and Individualism
detail.abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this paper is to understand the role of identity-based relationships, customer brand identification and peer identification, in driving customer outcomes including customer experiential hedonic value, social influence and repurchase intentions through the effects on value co-creation among customers and competitor brand hate, while taking into consideration the moderating impact of individualism. Design/methodology/approach – The study integrates social identity theory, identity-based marketing perspective and self-construal theory to develop relationships. The data comprises a web-based survey of customers in the USA and was analyzed using structural equation modeling. Findings – Customer brand identification and peer identification are drivers of value co-creation among customers, which leads to favorable outcomes at the customer and brand levels. Customer brand identification drives customers to hate competing brands, which, in turn, motivates customers to exert social influence in favor of their brand and to hold additional repurchase intentions. Customer brand identification and peer identification play different roles in motivating customers to co-create value with their fellows and drive customers to feel hatred toward competing brands contingent on customer individualism. Research limitations/implications – Customer brand identification and peer identification play different roles in engaging customers in value co-creation with their peers and competing brands have with their rivals. Individualism self-construal holds a dual role when interacting with customer identification. The study fills multiple gaps in the literature by examining additional effects of customer brand identification and peer identification and exploring a relatively new dimension of the value co-creation process, as well as the role of customers in the competition between brands. Practical implications – Brands need to view customers who identify with them as socially active customers capable of participating in value co-creation with other customers and engaging in the rivalry faced by the brands. Moreover, brands are required to build and nurture relationships that are based on social identification to encourage customer brand identification and peer identification which results in favorable customer and business outcomes. Originality/value – This study examines the effects of two forms of customer identification on value co-creation between customers and competitor brand hate. In addition, it identifies the dual moderating role of customer individualism on the effects of both social identification forms. The study fills multiple gaps in the literature by understanding new aspects of customer identification, value co-creation and brand hate.

title: Marketing AI Exposure: Applicability Breadth, Substitution Depth, and Job Outcomes
affiliations: , ,  and University of Georgia

detail.title: Marketing AI Exposure: Applicability Breadth, Substitution Depth, and Job Outcomes
detail.abstract: As AI reshapes organizational work, its overlap with marketing responsibilities raises questions about its impact on marketing jobs. This research introduces Marketing AI Exposure as a two-dimensional construct comprising AI applicability breadth and AI substitution depth. Applicability breadth captures the range of AI technologies relevant to a job’s task portfolio, whereas substitution depth captures the extent to which AI can perform those tasks. Using dependency parsing to extract verb-noun pairs from approximately 4.86 million marketing job postings and 1.3 million AI patents, we construct job posting-level measures of both dimensions. Regression analyses show that breadth is associated with higher hiring but lower wages, whereas depth is associated with lower hiring and lower wages. Jobs high on both dimensions show the strongest wage compression, but not uniform hiring contraction, underscoring the value of distinguishing AI availability from task coverage. The research also shows that marketing skills moderate these relationships heterogeneously.

title: Marketing The Vote: A Comparative Study of Political Marketing Techniques, Their Mechanisms, and their Effectiveness in Elections

detail.title: Marketing The Vote: A Comparative Study of Political Marketing Techniques, Their Mechanisms, and their Effectiveness in Elections
detail.abstract: Elections are increasingly fought and won using the tools and vocabulary of commercial marketing. This paper examines how political parties design and deploy marketing techniques-segmentation and positioning, branding, direct and relationship marketing, and data-driven microtargeting-to influence voter behaviour. Using India's Lok Sabha elections of 2014, 2019, and 2024 as the primary setting, and the Obama presidential campaigns of 2008 and 2012 as a comparative international benchmark, the paper traces the mechanics of each technique, the theoretical marketing frameworks that explain it, and the empirical evidence on how effective it actually is. The analysis draws on political marketing theory (Kotler, Lees-Marshment), campaign expenditure data disclosed to the Election Commission of India and Google's Ad Transparency Centre, and peer-reviewed experimental research on microtargeting. The paper finds that while digital and data-driven techniques have grown sharply in scale-Google ad spend by Indian parties rose roughly tenfold between 2019 and 2024-their persuasive effectiveness is more contested and context-dependent than campaign narratives suggest, with the strongest evidence for effects on turnout and voter retention rather than large-scale conversion of committed opposition voters.

title: Economic Dignity Infrastructure: The Agentive Reintegration Pathway
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Economic Dignity Infrastructure: The Agentive Reintegration Pathway
detail.abstract: Material stabilization within a dedicated institutional environment does not on its own produce societal reintegration. Individuals stabilized materially and relationally still face a competitive external labor market that penalizes résumé gaps institutional histories and the absence of normative identity capital. When stabilized residents attempt traditional labor market reentry they encounter the Return Deficit which is the aggregate compounding reduction in labor market returns produced by carrying multiple co-occurring stigmatized institutional markers simultaneously. This paper synthesizes established findings across multiple disciplines into a proposed institutional design. It develops a theoretical framework and specifies mechanisms intended for future empirical evaluation. It presents no new causal estimates. The paper introduces the Return Deficit as its principal theoretical contribution specifies the cooperative reintegration mechanism and the Tenancy Bridge Guarantee and identifies the failure modes that implementation must address. Detailed financial modeling is reserved for a subsequent working paper in this series.

title: Activating Corporate Environmental Ethics on the Frontline: A Natural Resource-Based View
affiliations: Auburn University,  and Iowa State-Ivy College of Business

detail.title: Activating Corporate Environmental Ethics on the Frontline: A Natural Resource-Based View
detail.abstract: Corporate environmental ethics has moved from a niche issue within business strategy to a potential source of competitive advantage. Firms, however, are comprised of individuals who vary in their personal beliefs regarding environmental responsibility. Environmental stewards are those employees whose attitudes and actions reflect environmental concern. Top management can convey similar environmental values through the creation of ecocapabilities. Applying logic from the natural resource-based view of the firm, we build a model to test how the alignment of environmental values impacts multiple outcomes. We conduct a time-lagged examination using multi-level data from frontline employees, their managers, and their customers. We find that firms can 'activate' their corporate environmental ethics through eco-capabilities. Specifically, environmental stewards find more meaning in their work when managers perceive high levels of eco-capabilities within the firm. This meaningful work increases employee brand advocacy and customer satisfaction. Together, we demonstrate how corporate environmental ethics translates to the frontline and the customers they serve.

title: Robots Went Where Workers Aged. Did AI? Demographic Labor Scarcity and the Direction of AI Adoption in Europe

detail.title: Robots Went Where Workers Aged. Did AI? Demographic Labor Scarcity and the Direction of AI Adoption in Europe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that she has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only publicly available, aggregate statistical data from Eurostat and the European Commission (DG ECFIN); no primary data collection involving human participants, patients, or personal/identifiable data was conducted.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Industrial robots diffused fastest where middle-aged manual workers were scarce (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2022). Does artificial intelligence follow the same demographic logic? Using Eurostat enterprise surveys (2021-2025, 32 European countries, 11 industries), I interact national demographic scarcity with industry-level occupational AI exposure under country-wave and industry-wave fixed effects. Two margins pull in opposite directions. Workforce aging predicts higher AI adoption in exposed industries-about 1.5 percentage points per standard deviation pair, a tenth of the mean-with no counterpart for pre-AI technologies and timing that coincides with the post-2021 generative-AI wave. Scarcity of young tertiary-educated workers, the labor AI most directly substitutes for, predicts lower adoption: complementarity in deployment dominates substitution. The evidence comes from an interaction design supported by fertility-history instruments, randomization inference on the exposure assignment, and concentration in cognitive AI technologies with null placebos; it is best read as strong suggestive evidence rather than definitive causal estimation. The offsetting margins explain why the raw aging-AI correlation across countries is flat. The evidence is consistent with factor scarcity directing technology adoption only when the scarce factor is not also the technology's operator.

title: Enhancing External Validity of Experiments with Ongoing Sampling
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, Faculty of Business and Economics, Students, The University of Hong Kong and Tencent Weixin Group

detail.title: Enhancing External Validity of Experiments with Ongoing Sampling
detail.abstract: Subjects in online experiments typically arrive and participate sequentially, which can compromise the external validity of experimental results due to temporal shifts in sample characteristics. This issue is particularly pronounced in A/B tests, which are often conducted over short durations to support rapid product decisions. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework that adapts to the dynamic nature of participant arrivals to improve external validity in online experimentation. Our method segments the ongoing sampling process into three distinct stages-unstable, overlapping, and representative-each corresponding to different levels of generalizability. Leveraging survival analysis, we develop a heuristic function that detects these stages in real time and enables the construction of stage-specific estimators for the population average treatment effect (PATE). We evaluate our framework using both a real-world A/B test and a platform-scale application involving 600 experiments conducted on WeChat, a major social media platform. The results show that our approach increases true positive decision rates by 28-37% while reducing false positive rates by 17-29%. We further provide evidence that the framework significantly influences experimentation practices-such as stopping decisions and experiment duration-following deployment, and we offer practical guidelines for implementation.

title: The Liberty Media Effect. How Narrative-Driven Personal Branding of Formula 1 Drivers Captures Gen Z Engagement

detail.title: The Liberty Media Effect. How Narrative-Driven Personal Branding of Formula 1 Drivers Captures Gen Z Engagement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently, and there are no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants in a way that required formal ethics approval. The research relied on publicly available social media data and a voluntary online survey. All survey participants provided implicit consent by voluntarily completing the questionnaire, and no personal or sensitive data was collected.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as an independent study by the author.

detail.abstract:
Formula 1's ownership under Liberty Media has repositioned the sport around entertainment and narrative content, with driver storytelling widely credited for the sport's growth among Generation Z audiences. This assumption, however, has rarely been tested directly against evidence of what drives engagement or against what younger fans themselves report as the basis of their loyalty. This thesis investigates whether, and how, narrative-driven personal branding of Formula 1 drivers contributes to Generation Z engagement and loyalty during the Liberty Media era, using a mixedmethods design that triangulates a quantitative content analysis of 180 driver social media posts with a survey of 306 Generation Z fans. 

The content analysis found that off-track, personality-driven content generates substantially higher engagement than on-track or commercial content (1,290,363 vs. 837,731 and 326,861 average Total Engagement per post, respectively), a pattern corroborated independently by the survey: 73.8 percent of respondents rated off-track content as strongly influencing their loyalty, and 61.4 percent entered the sport through Netflix's Drive to Survive or a driver's personal social media rather than broadcast television. However, individual post-level coding of authenticity and storytelling showed no meaningful correlation with engagement (r = 0.057 and r =-0.064 respectively), and fan loyalty proved sharply segmented: fans following personality-forward drivers reported mean loyalty-influence scores of 4.44-5.00 out of 5, against 1.72 for fans following the sport's most performance-focused driver. 

These findings support the central premise that Liberty Media's entertainment-driven repositioning of Formula 1 has succeeded in building engagement and loyalty among a substantial share of Generation Z fans, while showing that this effect is neither universal across the fan base nor detectable in the same way at every level of measurement-a distinction with direct implications for content strategy and for how athlete-branding research interprets engagement metrics more broadly.

title: Leveraging Marketing Campaign Data to Reverse-Engineer Corporate Strategy: A Framework for Dynamic Strategic Adjustment
affiliations: and

detail.title: Leveraging Marketing Campaign Data to Reverse-Engineer Corporate Strategy: A Framework for Dynamic Strategic Adjustment
detail.abstract: Traditional corporate strategy formulation follows a top-down, linear sequence: executives define long-term objectives, cascading down to functional tactics, with marketing campaigns typically serving as mere execution vehicles for predetermined plans. This study challenges that orthodox chronology by proposing and testing a reverse-engineered strategic framework in which marketing campaign data-traditionally considered an output of strategy-functions instead as a primary input for strategic revision. Employing a mixed-methods design, this research analyzes longitudinal campaign performance data (including customer acquisition costs, engagement metrics, sentiment analysis, and conversion funnels) from three mid-sized consumer goods firms over a 24-month period. Through computational pattern detection and qualitative interviews with senior strategists, we examine how emergent data anomalies, market signal shifts, and unpredicted consumer behaviors trigger iterative revisions to core strategic pillars, including resource allocation, product positioning, and market-entry timing. The findings reveal that algorithmic analysis of campaign data consistently identifies strategic inflection points 6-8 weeks earlier than conventional quarterly board reviews, enabling preemptive rather than reactive adjustments. We develop a Dynamic Strategic Adjustment Framework (DSAF) comprising four recursive stages: Signal Detection, Strategic Hypothesis Generation, Controlled Reallocation, and Performance Recalibration. The framework demonstrates that reversing the planning process does not undermine strategic coherence but rather enhances organizational agility by transforming marketing from a tactical function into a strategic sensing mechanism.

title: Time for Leisure, Mobility and Consumption Choices: Evidence from the Music Sector
affiliations: University of Warsaw

detail.title: Time for Leisure, Mobility and Consumption Choices: Evidence from the Music Sector

declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded with the National Science Centre OPUS research grant 2020/39/B/HS4/01015.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how constraints on time and attention relate to consumption choices, using the COVID-19 pandemic and its effects on mobility for identification. Linking Spotify and YouTube chart data with Google mobility indicators, I analyse how reduced commutingand thus increased leisure timerelated to both the volume of music consumption and the characteristics of selected content. Regression results with country and date fixed effects, as well as controls for pandemic severity and government restrictions on movement, support predictions from attention economics. Lower mobility is associated with fewer streams; but also with higher top chart prominence of songs with longer titles, greater acoustic diversity and older release dates. For YouTube, lower mobility also relates to popularity of longer videos with attention-intensity peaks positioned later. These patterns suggest that time constraints may reduce exploration and boost the need for quick gratification. My findings highlight the likely implications of the recent rise in supply of digital information goods on consumer decisions, which I frame within the context of attention economics and choice overload literature.

title: From Brand Fans to Devoted Consumers: Antecedents and Behavioral Outcomes of Brand Commitment in Kazakhstan's Fashion Market
affiliations: Ton Duc Thang University

detail.title: From Brand Fans to Devoted Consumers: Antecedents and Behavioral Outcomes of Brand Commitment in Kazakhstan's Fashion Market
detail.abstract: This study examines how consumers transition from being brand admirers to developing strong, enduring commitment toward fashion brands in the context of Kazakhstan's fashion market. Using survey data collected from fashion consumers, the results show that self-brand connection and relationship investment are significant drivers of brand commitment. Materialism and brand consciousness do not exert direct effects, but materialism influences commitment indirectly through self-brand connection, indicating that value orientations translate into commitment only when integrated into consumers' self-concepts. Brand commitment strongly predicts both behavioral loyalty and willingness to pay a premium. The study contributes to the literature by extending commitment-based frameworks to an underexplored emerging market and clarifying the identity-driven processes underlying brand relationships in fashion consumption.

title:
Profitability of Open-Source Software Product Development 
Forthcoming in Information Systems Research
affiliations: Southern Illinois University, , University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business and

detail.title:
Profitability of Open-Source Software Product Development 
Forthcoming in Information Systems Research
detail.abstract: For-profit firms increasingly adopt open-source product development by engaging external community members alongside internal employees on social coding platforms such as GitHub. Yet whether and through what mechanisms this engagement affects firm profitability remains an open question. Drawing on the knowledge-based view of the firm, we conceptualize open-source product development as a form of distributed knowledge integration that enhances labor productivity by expanding the specialized expertise available for product development beyond the firm's internal boundaries. We posit that improvements in labor productivity translate into higher profitability, as labor constitutes a primary input in software product development. However, the labor productivity effect depends on the extent of participation by external contributors, and the resulting profitability gains are shaped by equifinal configurations of firm resource allocation. We examine our theoretical framework using a longitudinal dataset of 977 U.S. high-tech firms from 2001 to 2025 and find that firms adopting open-source product development via GitHub realized, on average, a 4%-5% increase in gross margin. These results are robust across staggered difference-indifferences , generalized synthetic control, instrumental variable, and dynamic panel specifications. A moderated mediation analysis decomposing over 323,000 project-level contributions across more than 44,000 repositories into internal employee and external volunteer sources reveals that labor productivity partially mediates the profitability effect and that this mediation is amplified by external contributor engagement. The indirect effect of open-source development intensity on profitability through labor productivity becomes discernibly positive only beyond a threshold of external volunteer contributions (approximately 35% in our sample). Configurational analysis further reveals that research and development intensity is present across all highprofitability configurations, consistent with the absorptive capacity required to integrate externally sourced knowledge. These findings extend the knowledge-based view to the open-source context and provide managerial guidance for aligning open-source strategies with firms' resource configurations.

title: From Tellers to Tech: Labor Demand Shift and Bank Lending
affiliations: University of Basel - Faculty of Business and Economics and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: From Tellers to Tech: Labor Demand Shift and Bank Lending
detail.abstract: Using a novel measure of the composition of bank hiring, we examine how a labor demand shift affects bank lending. We find that the banks' demand shift toward higher-skilled labor is positively associated with lending. At the same time the banker-machine replacement also increases lending, through channels of operating efficiency, productivity, and lending capacity. This effect is stronger for banks that hire tech-bankers paying high wages. Conversely, lending shrinks for banks that reduce the number of relationship bankers. This effect is more concentrated among small banks and seems driven by declines in commercial and industrial loans. Overall, our findings indicate that the recent transformation in bank hiring expands credit supply, yet possibly also erodes relationship lending.

title: Trusting AI With Money: How Transaction Value, AI Autonomy, and Explainability Affect Consumer Trust and Willingness to Delegate Purchasing Decisions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trusting AI With Money: How Transaction Value, AI Autonomy, and Explainability Affect Consumer Trust and Willingness to Delegate Purchasing Decisions
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is moving beyond recommendation toward autonomous commercial action, allowing AI shopping agents to compare products, select alternatives, and potentially complete transactions on behalf of consumers. This study examined how transaction value, AI autonomy, and explainability affected consumer trust and willingness to delegate purchasing decisions. A randomised 2 × 3 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted using a hypothetical wireless-headphone purchase. Transaction value was manipulated at ฿500 or ฿15,000, autonomy was manipulated through recommendation-only, approval-required, and full-autonomy conditions, and explainability was manipulated by either providing or withholding a justification for the agent’s product selection. The final analytical sample consisted of 264 participants.

AI autonomy produced the strongest effect on willingness to delegate. Approval-required autonomy generated the highest willingness, whereas full autonomy produced the lowest willingness and perceived control. Participants were also less willing to delegate the high-value purchase than the low-value purchase, particularly when the agent operated with full autonomy. Explainability increased trust and produced a smaller increase in willingness, but it did not eliminate resistance to unrestricted purchasing authority. Previous AI experience was positively associated with willingness to delegate.

The findings distinguish trust in an AI recommendation from willingness to allow an AI system to spend money. They suggest that AI shopping systems may be more acceptable when they automate comparison and selection while preserving human approval for consequential transactions.

title: Data Governance as a Decision Variable: A Model-Driven Decision Support System for Budget Allocation in Generative AI Adoption
affiliations: ,  and University of Almería

detail.title: Data Governance as a Decision Variable: A Model-Driven Decision Support System for Budget Allocation in Generative AI Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human participants, no animal subjects and no personal data. The evaluation is based entirely on numerical simulation from a specified data-generating process; the complete replication package is openly available at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/LZTED5.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Corporate adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is routinely managed as a problem of technological scaling: firms decide how much to use the tool while treating the quality of the underlying knowledge base as a given feature of the environment. This paper shows that such a formulation is structurally incomplete and yields systematically biased recommendations. We present a model-driven decision support system (DSS) that endogenises data governance through an explicit budgetary variable, I Q , and that jointly solves the allocation between investment in information quality and the intensity of algorithmic use, x. The formal core is a non-linear, two-variable optimisation model in which data quality Q(I Q) simultaneously modulates the value production function and the cost structure, through a variable-cost coefficient γ(Q) and a convexity exponent δ (Q) that captures the agency cost of human oversightthe Babysitting Tax. We prove analytically the existence of a scissor effect (data degradation shifts marginal value downwards and marginal cost upwards at the same time), we characterise the Marginal Profit Destruction Zone, and we establish the existence of a viability corridor for governance investment, bounded both from below and from above. We further prove that, for firms with severely fragmented data architectures, Π * (I Q) is non-monotonic: the first units of governance investment reduce profit before increasing it, which gives the decision the character of a big push rather than of a marginal adjustment. On this core we build the artefact: a five-layer architecture-telemetry, estimation, optimisation, policy and interface-whose policy layer materialises in three executable budgetary decision rules (marginal parity, condition-precedent threshold and dynamic operating ceiling). We show that these three rules decentralise the centralised optimum between the Finance function and the Data function through the exchange of two scalars only, and that the convergence condition of the protocol coincides exactly with the second-order condition of the problem. The two-variable problem further reduces to a scalar search of logarithmic cost, which makes the artefact computable in real time. Simulation-based evaluation over two calibrated organisational profiles quantifies the value of the artefact: a firm with fragmented data that applies the conventional static model over-uses the technology by 27.8%, believes it is obtaining a profit of +32.0 monetary units and in fact realises a loss of 36.7, whereas the DSS solution places it at +8.4. The decomposition of the scissor effect reveals that the cost channel-ignored by the previous literature-accounts for a further contraction of the optimum of 91.7% on top of the contraction already caused by the loss of value.

title:
Decentralized Rail Platform Capacity Allocation under Congestion: 
A Dynamic Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) Auction with Token Taxation

detail.title:
Decentralized Rail Platform Capacity Allocation under Congestion: 
A Dynamic Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) Auction with Token Taxation

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, animals, or identifiable personal data. The research is based entirely on simulation, mathematical modeling, and synthetic railway operational data; therefore, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.

detail.abstract: Real-time disruption recovery in high-density railway networks requires resolving complex capacity allocation problems under tight timing constraints. Traditional dispatching models rely on centralized optimization, which struggles with scale during large disruptions and lacks the flexibility to manage multi-operator corridors where proprietary constraints cannot be shared. This paper presents a decentralized, game-theoretic multi-agent framework to allocate station platforms dynamically under network congestion. We model trains and station infrastructure as autonomous agents that negotiate platform track rights using a second-price Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction. Train agents compute bids using their passenger occupancy, service classes, and real-time delays to minimize network-wide passenger delay costs. To resolve the starvation problem common in budget-constrained VCG auctions where local services are persistently outbid by express trains we introduce a dynamic token taxation mechanism. Delayed trains accumulate token credits proportionally to their queue wait times, ensuring they eventually acquire platform access. We evaluate the mechanism on a simulated multi-corridor network representing the Mumbai-Ahmedabad and Mumbai-Pune high-speed corridors. The results indicate that while the VCG auction with dynamic token taxation maintains a controlled efficiencyfairness trade-off to accommodate local service priorities under physics-based catenary voltage drops, it successfully prevents local service starvation, stabilizes bidding budgets, and resolves interlocking conflicts efficiently without a centralized controller.

title: Synthetic Customer 360 Benchmark for Customer Data Quality, Identity Resolution, and Survivorship in Omnichannel Retail

detail.title: Synthetic Customer 360 Benchmark for Customer Data Quality, Identity Resolution, and Survivorship in Omnichannel Retail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study used only synthetic data and did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or biological materials.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for conducting this study.

detail.abstract: In omnichannel retail, customer data quality and unification architecture encompasses the systems and controls that turn fragmented customer observations into trusted, unified profiles, yet rigorous evaluation is constrained by limited access to shareable records with known identity, defect, datalineage, and survivorship ground truth. This paper presents a synthetic Customer 360 benchmark and generation method for controlled evaluation of identity resolution, data-quality transformations, and golden-record survivorship rules. The benchmark models persons, households, accounts, contact points, addresses, source observations, and transaction or order context across four profiles: ecommerce, loyalty or mobile, physical-store transaction, and service or fulfillment. It generates structural duplicates and eight auditable defect, ambiguity, and conflict mechanisms while preserving separate ground truth for duplicate clusters, transformation lineage, and expected outputs under verification-first, source-authority-first, recency-first, and mixed-conditional regimes. The study evaluates the benchmark through 335 predeclared runs organized into identity-difficulty, survivorship-conflict, single-factor-sensitivity, and scale experiments. Three transparent identity baselines are reported with pairwise and B-cubed measures; survivorship is assessed through applicability, evaluability, union and pairwise disagreement, conditional disagreement rate, and population-level burden. All 335 confirmatory runs passed validation. In 40 paired seeds, the easy identity condition exceeded the hard condition for weighted-similarity pairwise F1 at the primary 0.85 threshold, with a median paired difference of 0.5846 and a Holm-adjusted one-sided p value of 1.82 × 10 ¹². The direction held at predeclared thresholds of 0.80, 0.85, and 0.90. High-conflict ⁻ survivorship conditions exceeded low-conflict conditions in all 40 paired seeds, with a median conditional-disagreement increase of 0.0577 and the same adjusted p value. These findings demonstrate reproducible condition separation and auditable ground truth under the disclosed synthetic design. They do not establish real-retailer prevalence, operational effectiveness, production scalability, or universal superiority of any resolution or survivorship rule.

title: The Impact of Digitalisation on Inequalities: A Comparative Study across Nations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Digitalisation on Inequalities: A Comparative Study across Nations
detail.abstract:
This study analyses how digitalisation affects income inequality, through a cross- country econometric analysis covering 27 countries over the period 2000–2022. The analysis considers the impact of three key dimensions of digitalisation—Internet access, fixed broadband subscriptions and mobile phone services—on inequality, measured through the Gini index and the income shares held by different percentiles of the population.

From a methodological viewpoint, the study uses Generalized Least Squares (GLS) regression models, corrected for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation in panel data, combined with random effects models to account for unobservable heterogeneity between countries. Control variables such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita growth, demographic structure (young and working age population), urbanization rate and other economic-structural factors are included. The analysis was accompanied by extensive diagnostic tests (including VIF for multicollinearity and Wooldridge test), and robustness checks to strengthen the reliability of the estimates. Although the model reduces some risks of bias, it is acknowledged that it does not completely eliminate endogeneity problems, such as reverse causality between inequality and digitalization.

The paper tests three main hypotheses, based on the economic and sociological literature:

  • H1: Greater digital access reduces income inequality by expanding access to employment opportunities, financial services, education and healthcare, especially for low-income groups (Stern, M. J., 2009; George, G. & Schillebeeckx, J. D., 2022);

  • H2: The redistributive effect of digitalization is mediated by country-specific structural and institutional factors, such as educational systems, redistributive policies and digital literacy levels (Doric, Z., 2022);

  • H3: In countries where digital access is more widespread and inclusive (e.g. broadband infrastructure and mobile subscriptions), inequality is lower, especially in the lower deciles, indicating that digitalization can foster more equitable economic growth (Afzal, A. et al., 2023).

    The findings have important policy implications. To make digitalization an inclusive lever, public policies must go beyond the mere expansion of access, combining infrastructure investments with targeted initiatives on digital literacy, affordability, and technological endowment. Particular attention must be paid to the most vulnerable groups—such as low-income families or rural communities—who risk being excluded from the digital transition. Digital inclusion must be integrated into broader social and economic strategies to have a concrete redistributive impact.

    The study offers three main contributions. First, it proposes a comparative and longitudinal econometric model that integrates digital indicators in the analysis of inequalities. Second, it delves into the still little-explored mechanisms that link digitalization and inequality, highlighting the interaction with demographic and institutional variables. Third, it provides empirical evidence useful to support the design of more inclusive digital policies, calibrated to national contexts.

In conclusion, this study contributes to the global debate on the role of digitalization as a tool for inclusion or for reinforcing social inequalities. By offering a solid and empirically grounded comparative analysis, it supports the need for proactive digital policies that prioritize not only access, but also skills and the effective inclusion of the most vulnerable segments of the population.

title: The Cross-Layer Theory of Complexity: A General Framework for Understanding Emergence, Constraint, and Agency in Multi-Layered Complex Systems

detail.title: The Cross-Layer Theory of Complexity: A General Framework for Understanding Emergence, Constraint, and Agency in Multi-Layered Complex Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interests to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to declare

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a general theory of complexity grounded in a four-layer ontological architecture. The theory advances a central claim: genuine complexity emerges if and only if a system spans multiple ontological layers, where each layer is characterised by a distinct governance mode, agency degree, and thermodynamic regime. We identify four abstract layers-Elemental, Substantive, Cooperative, and Organized-that manifest at multiple scales from individual organisms to civilisational systems. Nineteen principles govern inter-layer relations, organised into six categories: layer structure, vertical relations, interfaces, temporality, energy dynamics, and agency. The framework generates a complexity typology distinguishing dissipative, adaptive, intentional, reflexive, and supra-intentional complexity based on layer span. We demonstrate the framework's analytical power through contrasting case studies (hurricane versus stock market) and address the question of whether artificial intelligence may constitute a fifth emergent layer. The theory provides predictive capacity absent from existing frameworks, including Donella Meadows' leverage points and David Snowden's Cynefin, by grounding the simple-complicated-complex distinction in ontological layer structure.

title: Correlated Intelligence: AI Adoption and Systemic Risk
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: Correlated Intelligence: AI Adoption and Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: Banks delegate decisions to AI models from a common vendor frontier that bundles accuracy with error correlation: the most accurate models share lineage and fail together. The cross-bank cost of that correlation remains unpriced even when lineage is observable, because a credit spread reprices the borrower, not the banks its choice endangers. Model diversity is inefficiently low; under pooled pricing, welfare losses grow quadratically with excess adoption. Frontier improvements can reduce welfare by tipping the market into monoculture. Disclosure makes a correlation surcharge feasible but does not substitute for it.

title: A Domain-Specific Causal Chain RAG System for Semiconductor Equity Analysis

detail.title: A Domain-Specific Causal Chain RAG System for Semiconductor Equity Analysis
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) applied to equity analysis frequently suffer from shallow reasoning: they surface correlated market signals without modeling the causal mechanisms that connect macroeconomic conditions to firm-level outcomes. This paper presents SemiBot, an agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that scores semiconductor equities across an 18-factor causal chain spanning macroeconomic, fundamental, market-intelligence, and external-signal categories. SemiBot combines a LangGraph multi-agent orchestration layer, a FAISS-backed causal-chain retriever, real-time data acquisition via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Tavily search, and SQLite-based long-term memory to produce ticker-level directional predictions with per-factor attribution. We describe the system's architecture and three engineering failure modes discovered during development, together with their resolutions. We evaluate SemiBot through three complementary backtests.
