Backtest 1, using 140 valid predictions accumulated from development-period usage, shows 61.4% directional accuracy under an MA50 price-proxy and 69.3% under an MA200 proxy (a disclosed sensitivity check, not a precise point estimate). Backtest 2, a deliberately designed experiment on SemiBot's finalized 48-ticker production universe at 10 stratified historical dates with a genuine fixed 20-trading-day forward-return outcome (426 valid observations), shows 61.3% overall directional accuracy. Critically, accuracy is strongly and monotonically related to market capitalization: mega-cap tickers (>$200B) achieve 77.2% accuracy versus 41.7% for mid-cap tickers ($2B-$10B), with a clean six-tier breakdown ranging from 84.0% (>$1 trillion) down to 41.7% (<$10B). This relationship is statistically confirmed via logistic regression (β=0.327, p<0.001) and a chi-square test comparing the mega- and mid-cap tiers directly (χ²=26.32, p<0.001), with 95% confidence intervals reported for every tier, and is shown to be robust to controlling for sub-sector composition (β=0.291, p<0.001) and to persist, albeit at reduced magnitude, even on the sample's weakest-performing dates. Backtest 3 tests SemiBot against two naive baselines — an Always-UP strategy and a SOXX prior-trend-following strategy — stratified across the same six market-capitalization tiers as Backtest 2, using the identical 426-observation production dataset. Against Always-UP, SemiBot underperforms in every tier (overall 61.3% vs. 76.8%, a 15.5-point gap, narrowing from 29.1 points at the smallest tier to 2.0 points at the largest). Against the more sophisticated SOXX-trend baseline, the picture is more nuanced: SemiBot underperforms overall (61.3% vs. 66.9%) but outperforms in its two largest tiers — by 8.0 points at >$1 Trillion and 5.7 points at $500B–$1T — while underperforming at every tier below $500B. This is, to our knowledge, the first market-capitalization-stratified naive-baseline comparison reported for a causal-chain equity-analysis system, and it demonstrates that whether causal-chain reasoning adds value over naive momentum depends jointly on company size and on which naive strategy is used as the comparison point — a nuance a single aggregate accuracy figure, or a single unstratified baseline comparison, would entirely conceal. We situate these results against directly comparable literature benchmarks (Ploutos-7B: 61.2%/59.9%; Vidal 2024's 250-stock LLM study: 59.4% average; TRACE: 55.1%; a "Crystal Ball" human-trader experiment: 51.5%), finding SemiBot's mega-cap and >$1 Trillion subsets exceed every comparable published figure. We argue that explicit causal-chain scaffolding produces interpretable, well-attributed equity signals with genuine, quantifiable value at the largest end of the market-capitalization spectrum, and that market-capitalization-stratified naive-baseline comparison — not literature benchmarking alone — should be standard practice for evaluating this class of system.

title: Best Practices for University-Startup Partnerships: A Teaching Tip
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Best Practices for University-Startup Partnerships: A Teaching Tip
detail.abstract: Universities can benefit from partnerships with startup companies by gaining access to new industry technology and expertise. These partnerships also ensure that academic programs remain relevant to industry and provide professional preparation for students. Universities may also enhance their research capabilities and funding opportunities through industry partnerships. Likewise, startup companies benefit from these collaborations through exposure to diverse perspectives on product-market fit and product development. Startups also gain increased access to a talented academic workforce. Based on the experiences of a project between a US university and a financial technology startup company, we suggest several practical tips and suggestions that both faculty and startup professionals can adopt for future collaborations.

title:
Scoring the Pushback, Not the Decision: 
A Deterministic Index of Challenge Intensity in an AI Cognitive Contradictor — the Δ-CSI (Cognitive Sovereignty Index, delta)

detail.title:
Scoring the Pushback, Not the Decision: 
A Deterministic Index of Challenge Intensity in an AI Cognitive Contradictor — the Δ-CSI (Cognitive Sovereignty Index, delta)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author develops CounterBrain, the commercial cognitive-contradictor platform in which the Delta-CSI specified here is implemented. The paper makes no claim of empirical validity or effectiveness for the index, and reports its declared weaknesses in Section 7.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable: this research involved no human subjects and no personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Decision-making under intensive AI assistance faces a documented paradox: more analysis does not reliably produce better judgment, because assistants optimized for user satisfaction tend to confirm rather than contest, inflating confidence and homogenizing reasoning across the organizations that share them. There is a structurally adversarial alternative: a cognitive contradictor, whose function is to challenge a decision rather than validate it. It raises an immediate measurement question. How does one quantify how hard a decision was contested, in a way that is reproducible in its scoring, comparable over time, and honest about what it does and does not establish? This paper defines that quantity. It introduces the Δ-CSI (Cognitive Sovereignty Index, delta) as a construct — the intensity of the structured challenge applied to a single decision in a single analysis session — and specifies its operational definition. The Δ-CSI is a deterministic index in [0, 100], computed from five weighted components: implicit-assumption count modulated by mean severity, falsification-test count, burden-of-proof-question count, cited-source count, and thesis-versus-counter-scenario divergence. Counts are capped, which precludes gaming by verbosity. Weights are constrained to sum to one hundred, interpretation bands are fixed, and the versioning scheme is explicit. Two limits remain, and are stated openly: the self-reported severity channel is gameable by construction (§7), and the count components register quantity, not argument quality. The paper contributes three things. (i) The construct, delimited by four negations: challenge intensity is not decision quality, not the probability of success, not a verdict on the decision-maker, and not whether the decision was subsequently changed. (ii) The specification, together with its reproducibility guarantee, its fail-closed defenses against sycophantic output, and a register of its declared weaknesses. (iii) The comparability and calibration discipline: cohorts keyed by computation version, divergence method, and weights, with statistics held to descriptive-only below five recorded outcomes. The paper makes no claim of empirical validity or effectiveness. It does not assert that a high Δ-CSI corresponds to better decisions — nor, conversely, to weaker ones — and it does not assert that the index predicts outcomes; it demonstrates construct definition and measurement method only. Empirical validation is stated as a deferred programme, structured as a pre-registered evidence-accumulation roadmap. Its two stages are per-tenant ledger calibration and the public sealed M&A pilot of the companion Calibrated Dissent, in which the Δ-CSI enters strictly as non-scoring provenance and an exploratory covariate. We treat this honesty as a design requirement, not a caveat: an index of challenge intensity that overstated its own validation would be inconsistent with the very stance it exists to measure.

title: Observation-Centered Runtime Safety for Foundation-Model Agents: A Model-Agnostic Geometry–Risk–Control Architecture

detail.title: Observation-Centered Runtime Safety for Foundation-Model Agents: A Model-Agnostic Geometry–Risk–Control Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The work was conducted by the authors as part of research activities at Gemmina Intelligence LLC. The authors declare that no external commercial entity influenced the design, implementation, interpretation, or reporting of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work did not involve human participants, animals, or clinical data, and therefore did not require institutional ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Alignment research for large language models has focused primarily on model-centric interventions-fine-tuning, preference optimization, and decoding-time filters. These methods improve average behavior, yet they do not continuously observe or constrain the runtime trajectory of an agent as it acts in a tool-using environment. We present an observationcentered runtime safety architecture that treats semantic state as a measurable trajectory and separates safety into five strictly layered concerns: Observation, Geometry, Risk, Control, and (future) Execution. The architecture is realized as the SensOS Runtime Safety Layer through a staged experimental program. Heterogeneous agent events are normalized into an Observation Object and projected to a trajectory; a model-agnostic geometry engine estimates curvature, boundary distance, density, stability, and basin membership; a risk engine converts those descriptors into a continuous risk valuation with hysteresis and early warning; and a control engine maps risk to a graduated L0-L7 decision under an approval interlock. Execution against a live agent is intentionally excluded: control outputs are decisions only, pending a separate safety review. On a real Claude Code session (n = 489 events), end-to-end observation pipeline latency was 0.094 ms mean per event (alert-only; zero alerts at threshold 0.5). Geometry, risk, and control packages exhibit production-grade software engineering quality-full statement and branch test coverage (95/151/107 tests)-with measured sub-millisecond risk and control latencies (0.0067/0.0039 ms mean). These figures characterize software quality and microbenchmarks, not validated operational safety. We do not claim live intervention efficacy; we claim a coherent, measured, and architecturally honest decision spine for runtime safety without modifying foundation models.

title: The Checking Problem: What Must Be True Before AI Ships in a Regulated Firm

detail.title: The Checking Problem: What Must Be True Before AI Ships in a Regulated Firm
detail.abstract: Enterprise AI programmes stall at a rate that is widely quoted and poorly explained. This paper measures the mechanism. Six document-heavy workflows of the kind performed daily in regulated financial services were run across four model families and three tool configurations, three times each, producing 5,093 scored output elements across 72 configurations. Each configuration was assessed twice: against a demonstration bar, being a single correct run on a single case, and against a production bar requiring sustained accuracy, reproducibility across repeats, verifiable attribution, and a confidence signal that carries information. 57 of 72 configurations cleared the demonstration bar and 32 cleared the production bar, a survival rate of 56.1%. The paper then computes the review burden each configuration imposes, estimated out of sample rather than with hindsight. A tool that states no confidence requires review of 100% of its output, because it offers a reviewer no basis for triage. Requiring the tool to cite its sources and state a confidence reduces that to 49% while holding the residual error tolerance in 17 of 20 configurations. Adding a self-verification pass costs 2.3 times the latency of the plain configuration, reaches 44%, and is the only configuration that fails to hold the error tolerance. The practical implication is that the value of an AI workflow is set less by how often it is right than by how much of it a human must still check, and that the second property is measurable and rarely measured.

title: Non-debt Money Anchored to Realized Value: A New Model of Money Issuance Defining the Measure of Value in the Age of Technological Acceleration
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Non-debt Money Anchored to Realized Value: A New Model of Money Issuance Defining the Measure of Value in the Age of Technological Acceleration
detail.abstract: Modern money is created before value is realized. Central banks issue against promises — the repayment of public debt, the acceptance of taxes — and the issuance mechanism never verifies whether the money corresponds to realized value. In the AI era this produces five problems: the breakdown of the labor–income–consumption distribution channel, deficient demand and deflation, monetary transmission failure, the fiscal deadlock of UBI, and the payment-term malaise of supply-chain finance. This paper reverses the sequence: money is created only after value is realized. When a verified good reaches a verified consumer, the delivery event itself triggers issuance, and smart contracts distribute it through the supply chain in the same instant. We develop an ontology of money — whether money must be repaid depends on whether it records a promise or a fact — showing that every historical promise-anchor (treasury debt, taxation, real bills) is an issuer's liability, while a verified delivery event is the first anchor that is nobody's liability and anchors realized value itself. Money is the measure of value already produced, not of value that might be produced. A value theory follows: production is the necessary condition, demand the finalizer, and AI splits output value from irreducibly human demand value. A minimal formal model proves five propositions: event-level non-overissue, sufficient conditions for inflation elimination, the ontological difference from credit issuance, a reversed Cantillon effect, and the quota's black-market immunity. We detail the mechanism design, a data-based inflation analysis, comparisons with UBI, MMT, CBDC, the real bills doctrine and social credit theory, an implementation path for China, the US and the UK, a policy-feasibility analysis, and answers to the seven strongest objections. Claims are restricted to falsifiable mechanism properties; far-future institutional forms are marked as directional speculation only.

title: Hallucination in Generative AI as Evaluative and Institutional Misalignment: The Hallucination-Institutional Nexus and Institutional Calibration

detail.title: Hallucination in Generative AI as Evaluative and Institutional Misalignment: The Hallucination-Institutional Nexus and Institutional Calibration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Hallucination in generative AI is often understood as a model-level failure involving inaccurate, unsupported, or fabricated outputs. While this view remains important, it is insufficient to explain why such outputs acquire institutional consequences when used in professional advice, evaluation, organizational decision-making, or other contexts in which justification, verification, judgment, and responsibility are required. This paper proposes the Hallucination-Institutional Nexus (HIN) as a conceptual framework for analyzing this transition. It first introduces the YMCK framework, which understands AI-mediated output as emerging through the interaction of Yardstick, Metacognition, Cognition, and Knowledge under specific contextual conditions. On this basis, HIN is defined as the structural interface at which AI-generated outputs become institutionally significant by entering regimes of evaluation, verification, judgment, and responsibility. This paper complements, rather than replaces, technical research on hallucination. The paper argues that, in institutional contexts, hallucination should not be understood solely as a model-level error, but as an evaluative and institutional misalignment between AI-generated output and the institutional structures in which that output is used as grounds for action or judgment. Mitigation therefore requires not only model-level improvement, but also institutional calibration: the adjustment of evaluation criteria, verification procedures, stopping conditions, responsibility boundaries, and recordable processes before AI-generated output is connected to institutional judgment. The paper concludes that hallucination should be understood as a structural signal indicating the need to calibrate the institutional conditions under which generative AI is evaluated and used.

title: Organization of Platform Markets: Coordination, Decision Rights and Information
affiliations: University of Utah -- Eccles School of Business and

detail.title: Organization of Platform Markets: Coordination, Decision Rights and Information
detail.abstract: Platform markets differ fundamentally from traditional firms, relying on decentralized supply of services by diverse, independent agents. Agents operate with limited information and compete to maximize their own profits. This structural shift raises critical questions about the optimal organization of platforms to coordinate the efforts of distributed participants. Should decision making in a platform market be centralized or decentralized, i.e., controlled by the platform or by agents? To study this question, we define the coordination structure (CS) of the platform market as the combination of two elements: its decision rights structure ('who decides what') and information endowment ('who knows what'). We focus on the pricing decision, which epitomizes both coordination and information challenges in platform governance. We model a platform with competing agents facing demand uncertainty that can be partly alleviated through information. We model different facets of information endowment, including local and aggregate intelligence, the ability to acquire and share intelligence, and non-transferable specific knowledge of both the platform and agents. We find that centralized coordination of prices, enabled by centralized CS, is a powerful lever for improving platform performance. Indeed, centralized CS dominates decentralized CS, reversing the results of the extant literature on traditional firms. The value of centralized coordination increases rapidly with the degree of agent competition. While decentralized CS can outperform centralized CS when agents hold significant informational advantages over the platform, this advantage diminishes rapidly as agent competition increases. We also demonstrate that centralized CS harnesses information more effectively to reinforce coordination and maximize profits.

title: Eighteen Frameworks, No Evidence A Systematic Multivocal Review of Enterprise AI use-case Prioritization

detail.title: Eighteen Frameworks, No Evidence A Systematic Multivocal Review of Enterprise AI use-case Prioritization
detail.abstract: Selecting which use cases to pursue is among the most consequential decisions in enterprise artificial intelligence, yet the guidance that shapes this decision in practice has never been examined systematically. This paper reports a systematic multivocal review of the publicly accessible use-case prioritization frameworks published by the organizations that dominate enterprise AI discourse. Eighteen framework artifacts from model vendors, cloud vendors, analysts, consultancies, and boutique experts (including OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Gartner, McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte, EY, and PwC) were identified through a documented search protocol and coded against a theory-grounded codebook covering four decision dimensions (value, feasibility, risk, adoptability) and four process disciplines (ownership, portfolio logic, gates and stopping conditions, weighted scoring). Three findings stand out. First, coverage is deeply uneven: value is an explicit criterion in seventeen of eighteen frameworks, but the human dimension of adoption is operationalized in only five, and the question of who owns the initiative in only three. Second, process discipline is scarce: only two artifacts articulate stopping conditions for running initiatives, and eleven specify no scoring method at all. Third, and most striking, not one of the eighteen frameworks presents evidence that its use improves selection outcomes. The paper documents additional quality defects of the guidance ecosystem itself, including a misattributed report and methods gated behind lead-generation forms. The results substantiate, with data, the selection blind spot conjectured in prior work, and they define a concrete agenda: the empirical validation that this entire class of instruments currently lacks.

title: Multimodal Measurement of Cognitive Load in Instructional Videos
affiliations: , Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management, Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management  and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Multimodal Measurement of Cognitive Load in Instructional Videos
detail.abstract: Digital learning platforms have become a fundamental interface between learners and educational content, making it critical to understand how platform design shapes learner engagement and performance. This study investigates how video and instructor characteristics, cognitive load, and learner behavior interact to influence engagement and academic outcomes in online learning environments. We develop a multimodal, theory-guided pipeline that measures cognitive load directly from instructional video content, extracting visual, auditory, and textual features and mapping them to intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load. Applying this pipeline to a unique large-scale dataset from Outlier.org, spanning over 1,200 instructional videos and more than 14,000 learners across 14 subjects, we examine how different components of cognitive demand relate to learner engagement and performance. Our results show that while learners exhibit demographic preferences in instructor selection, these preferences do not reliably translate into better performance; instead, content-based cognitive load, measured directly from video, is a robust indicator of engagement and learning, highlighting the potential for real-time, AI-driven interventions to provide adaptive scaffolding. Our findings offer actionable insights for platform designers and educators, advocating for dynamic, modular video content and behavior-aware personalization to enhance learning outcomes at scale.

title: Synthetic Hegemony: Generative AI and the Democratic Risks of Language Infrastructure

detail.title: Synthetic Hegemony: Generative AI and the Democratic Risks of Language Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, financial or personal.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual article involving no human subjects or participants. A separately planned empirical study will be contingent on institutional review board (IRB) approval.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This article introduces hybrid barbarism as a concept with two co-present modalities and theorizes their convergence under generative artificial intelligence. Hybrid barbarism is a persistent public-sphere pathology in which algorithmic infrastructures amplify emotive tribalism while the civic norms of shared inquiry atrophy. Platformized media sediment a distribution modality (HB-D) that rewards circulation; language-synthesis systems add a generation modality (HB-S) that assembles plausibility at the moment of production. Their interlocking generation–distribution–re-generation loop erodes shared facts, blurs provenance, and overloads institutions designed for fixed objects and stable authorship. I identify three mechanisms distinctive to HB-S — epistemic delegation, synthetic neutrality, and authorlessness — and specify the boundary conditions under which each becomes pathological rather than benign or even corrective. Reading three democratic contexts (the United States and Brazil; South Korea; Hungary and Turkey) through the framework, I derive three strategic manifestations — epistemic fragmentation, institutional sabotage, and systemic control — and state the conditions that select among them. Against approaches that merely police “bad content,” I argue for a Democratic Epistemic Infrastructure: public-interest language models with auditable lineage, civic AI literacy that restores critical distance, and risk-based provenance and audit regimes in high-stakes domains. The article is a concept paper; the case readings are advanced as derived expectations rather than demonstrated findings, and a separate preregistered empirical study is designed to render the claims falsifiable and cumulative.

title: Explainable AI Framework for Early Prediction of Cost Overruns in U.S. Mega Infrastructure Projects
affiliations: Ain Shams University Cairo

detail.title: Explainable AI Framework for Early Prediction of Cost Overruns in U.S. Mega Infrastructure Projects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or conflicts of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Large-scale infrastructure projects play a critical role in supporting economic growth, improving transportation systems, enhancing public services, and promoting national competitiveness. Governments in the United States invest hundreds of billions of dollars annually in transportation, water, energy, and public infrastructure projects to address aging assets and meet increasing societal demands. Despite these substantial investments, cost overruns remain one of the most persistent challenges affecting the successful delivery of infrastructure projects.
Cost overruns occur when the actual project cost exceeds the initially approved budget and has been widely reported across various infrastructure sectors worldwide. Studies have shown that transportation, highway, railway, bridge, and public works projects frequently experience significant deviations from planned budgets, resulting in financial losses, delays, reduced project scope, and diminished public confidence. In the United States, cost overruns have become a major concern for government agencies, project owners, contractors, and taxpayers due to their adverse impact on resource allocation and infrastructure development programs.
Numerous factors contribute to cost overruns in mega infrastructure projects. Common causes include scope changes, design modifications, inaccurate cost estimation, inflation, material price volatility, labor shortages, contractor performance issues, unforeseen site conditions, and schedule delays. The increasing complexity of modern infrastructure projects further amplifies the uncertainty associated with project execution, making accurate cost forecasting a challenging task for project managers and decision-makers.

Therefore, this study aims to develop an Explainable AI framework for the early prediction of cost overruns in U.S. mega infrastructure projects. Specifically, the study seeks to compare the predictive performance of several machine learning algorithms, identify the most influential cost overrun drivers, and establish an interpretable early warning system that can assist project stakeholders in mitigating financial risks during project execution.

title: Productivity of commerce in the time of AI and e-commerce
affiliations: University of Szczecin - Institute of Management and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Productivity of commerce in the time of AI and e-commerce
detail.abstract: The authors analyzed the financial results of 219 retail, wholesale, and e-commerce companies from the US and EU to calculate the productivity of employees, stores and inventories over a 15-year period. The results indicate that the productivity of American companies (retail, wholesale companies, as well as e-commerce) is higher than European companies, and that the productivity of international trading companies is usually higher than that of single-country companies. Employee productivity in wholesale companies is the highest, average in e-commerce, and lowest in retail. The sales volume does not have a significant impact on productivity – only in some sectors the largest firms are also the most productive. Type of business activity is important factor on productivity. The pandemic period had little impact on productivity, revenue, and employment. The implementation of modern technologies does not translate into significant productivity gains, employment reductions, or improved financial results.

title: Quality Assessment and User Adoption Prediction for Enterprise -Level Financial Reporting Data Products
affiliations: Columbia University, Johns Hopkins University, George Washington University and University of College London

detail.title: Quality Assessment and User Adoption Prediction for Enterprise -Level Financial Reporting Data Products
detail.abstract: Enterprise-level financial reporting data products combine transaction details, accounting accounts, tax dimensions, product definitions, refresh records, and user-access evidence. Existing approaches usually evaluate table-level data quality, analyze financial reports, or predict technology adoption as separate tasks; they rarely connect field semantics, executable validation results, user acceptance testing (UAT) evidence, and post-release behavior through the same traceable field identifier. This paper does not claim a new standalone Sentence-BERT, Great Expectations, LightGBM, or SHAP algorithm. Its contribution lies in a field-keyed integrated workflow for financial reporting delivery, a closed-loop remediation mechanism that maps model outputs to responsible fields and standard operating procedure (SOP) nodes, and empirical deployment evidence from an enterprise reporting environment. The workflow integrates transaction details, product dimensions, accounting accounts, tax fields, user query logs, UAT defect records, refresh records, report-access behavior, and SOP execution records. Sentence-BERT is used to align requirement documents, field descriptions, and UAT feedback; Great Expectations is used to execute dataquality rules; LightGBM estimates the probability of stable user adoption; and SHAP provides model-attribution evidence for release review. The deployment dataset contains 12 financial reporting products, 860 core fields, 2,400 mapping rules, 1,700 UAT feedback entries, 21 months of access logs, 46 million transaction records, 38 rule categories, 12 cross-departmental SOP procedures, and six reporting use cases. Sentence-BERT achieved 91.9% precision in identifying field semantic conflicts, and LightGBM achieved an AUC of 0.936 for adoption prediction. After the standardized workflow was introduced, the observed adoption rate increased from 10% to 80%, monthly active analytical users increased from 34 to 216, duplicate field-definition verification tickets decreased from approximately 145 to 39 per month, average UAT defect-resolution time decreased from 9.2 to 2.8 days, and the delivery cycle decreased from 11 to 5 weeks. These before-and-after changes are descriptive associations rather than causal estimates, because concurrent organizational and process changes may also have contributed. The results indicate that an integrated, traceable evidence chain can support earlier identification of field conflicts, quality defects, and adoption risk while preserving auditability in financial data governance.

title: Blockage Early Warning and Financial Impact Quantification in the Monthly Closing Process of Fintech Companies
affiliations: Columbia University, George Washington University, University of College London and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Blockage Early Warning and Financial Impact Quantification in the Monthly Closing Process of Fintech Companies
detail.abstract: For fintech companies, the monthly closing process includes several key phases, such as the release of trading, the updating of data, the distribution of profit and loss, the creation of journal entries, and the delivery of financial statements. In a high-volume transaction environment, data delays, inadequate journal entry, P&L allocation anomalies, and system task failures can easily lead to closure bottlenecks and impact on the timeliness of financial report.This study is a terminal process as a task-dependent network and provides a model for early warning of blockage closure and quantification of financial effects, utilizing a closure schedule, task completion times, transaction data update status, system fault log, journal entry evidence, P&L assignment rules, and monthly review records as core variables.The study uses a Temporal Fusion Transformer to predict the risk of task delay over the next 24 to 72 hours, using a Bayesian network to model conditional dependencies among data updates, system task failures, missing journal entries, and cross-team responses, and a combination of Random Forest algorithms to evaluate the severity of the effects of an unusual event on the closing time and the delivery of the financial statement.The experimental data set includes 36 months of closure period, 420 closing task nodes, 2,800 system exception records, 35 million transaction details, 18 types of P&L assignment rules, 7 600 journal entries, and 12 closing impact scenarios. In the observational pre-and post-deployment comparison, implementation of the joint model was associated with a decrease in blockage localization time from 31.0 h to 6.5 h. High-risk tasks could be marked 1 to 3 days in advance; the monthly number of journal entry documents requiring manual consolidation decreased from about 220 to 78; and annual repetitive journal entry processing time decreased by more than 350 h. Because the comparison was not randomized, these operational changes are interpreted as deployment-associated outcomes rather than controlled causal effects. The Bayesian network has identified three main blocking paths: data refresh delay, system task failure, and P&L assignment rule anomaly. The Random Forest achieves an accuracy of 90.9% for the identification of events with high financial effects.This study converts the monthly closure from a linear task list into a predictable process risk net, which allows the financial group to identify the source of the blockage, evaluate the extent of the impact, and prepare a journal entry document prior to the closure. The findings can increase the timeliness of financial reporting, the effectiveness of close cooperation, and the availability of data for management analysis by fintech firms.

title: Hiring Less, Keeping More? A Firm-Level Study of Labor Dynamics in AI-Focused Mergers and Acquisitions
affiliations: , Lehigh University, University of Georgia - Department of Management Information Systems and Beijing Foreign Studies University

detail.title: Hiring Less, Keeping More? A Firm-Level Study of Labor Dynamics in AI-Focused Mergers and Acquisitions
detail.abstract: Although the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on labor markets has been extensively studied, the labor consequences of AI-focused mergers and acquisitions (AI-M&As) remain underexplored. AI-M&As represent an external pathway through which firms acquire AI capabilities. It is different from internal AI adoption in that technological transformation arrives together with the organizational turbulence inherent in acquisitions. We use supervised machine learning to identify 3,149 AI-M&As between 2008 and 2023, and estimate their effects using a stacked difference-indifferences design. The results reveal an organizational stabilization effect rather than a mass labor displacement effect. Compared with non-AI-M&As, AI-M&As slow the growth of external hiring by 4.1% and that of employee departure by 5.3%, while total employment growth is statistically similar. The slowdown in departure is driven primarily by voluntary quits, which grow 4.0% more slowly, while involuntary layoffs do not differ significantly across the two groups. These effects are concentrated in entry-level positions on the hiring (-2.8%) and in middle management on departure (-2.3%). Additionally, these effects are strongest in finance, operations, and engineering functions. Overall, the evidence suggests that AI-M&As reorganize internal labor markets toward lower turnover rather than producing job losses as concerned in the separate literatures of AI research and M&A research.

title: Data Quality Monitoring and Intelligent Scheduling Optimization in Financial Data Workflow Automation
affiliations: Columbia University, George Washington University, Johns Hopkins University and University of College London

detail.title: Data Quality Monitoring and Intelligent Scheduling Optimization in Financial Data Workflow Automation
detail.abstract: Many sources of data workflows are available to fintech companies and large-scale digital platforms for financial reporting, audits, tax accounting, operations, etc. Problems such as task failure, field drift, data delay and inconsistencies in data definition can negatively impact monthly closings, report generation and the reliability of audit evidence. This study focuses on data quality monitoring and operational efficiency optimisation for financial data workflow automation, integrating Airflow task logs, SQL execution results, data table refresh status, changes in field distribution, report access records, manual repair records and exception ticket information into a unified monitoring system. LogBERT is used to identify anomalous semantics in task logs, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and DBSCAN are employed to detect field distribution drift and abnormal null value patterns; deep reinforcement learning models are introduced to optimise task scheduling priorities and ensure that critical financial reports, audit datasets and operational analysis tasks are completed first under resource constraints. The experimental dataset includes more than 40 Python/Airflow data pipelines, 120 scheduled reporting tasks, 9 source systems, 18 months of workflow logs, 210 million task execution and data quality records, 860 core financial fields, 38 categories of data quality rules, and about 6,500 manual repair records. The results show that LogBERT achieved a classification accuracy of 93.4% for the root causes of task failures; field drift detection issued early warnings an average of 6.8 hours before data anomalies reached downstream reports; and DBSCAN achieved an 89.7% recall rate for identifying abnormal null value combinations. The deep reinforcement learning scheduling strategy reduced the average delay of critical reports by 36.8%, lowered monthly manual inspection tasks from about 1,200 to 430, shortened the average data issue resolution time from 14.2 hours to 4.6 hours, and reduced repetitive manual verification time by 52.1%. Compared with traditional scheduled processing and manual spot checks, this method includes log semantics, field distributions, task priorities and manual remediation feedback in a closed-loop optimisation process to transform financial data workflows from reactive fault handling to proactive quality monitoring and intelligent scheduling. Research has provided support for improving the stability and traceability of financial data workflows to establish a high-quality data foundation for financial reporting, audit support, tax analysis and other data-driven operations by financial technology companies.
